title: ESC Heart Failure: A New Journal Aims to Broaden Heart Failure Views
abstract: ESC Heart Failure, the new daughter journal of the European Journal of Heart Failure, was launched in September 2014 and is published by Wiley on behalf of the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC). The journal is set up to cover a broad range of articles with the topic of heart failure (HF) in its broadest sense. These articles include original research articles, review articles, editorial comments, case reports, letters to the Editor, and meeting highlights. In addition, the journal aims to cover not only clinical research, but indeed all aspects of HF including basic research reports from subcellular and cellular structures, to animal research, to research on biomarkers, pathophysiology, diagnostic and imaging procedures, to clinical intervention trials. The aim of this Viewpoint is to provide a short overview of what the ESC Heart Failure is publishing and to show a few highlights that have been published in it recently. Ponikowski et al.1 highlighted in an HFA white paper the burden of HF that currently affects ∼6 million people worldwide, stating that the outlook of patients is poor, with survival rates that are several times worse than those for cancer patients.2 Several papers in ESC Heart Failure have highlighted the importance of HF in Asia.3, 4 Lam5 points out the strikingly high prevalence of HF in stage A, with >24% of people in Cambodia and Laos having hypertension as a risk factor for HF development—corresponding numbers in the UK and the USA only reach 13–15%. Similar differences are being reported for tobacco smoking, physical inactivity, and raised blood glucose levels, which prompts the author to state that the prevalence of symptomatic HF is much higher in Southeast Asian countries than in the rest of the world. Two recent reports provide information on the epidemiology of HF in the Middle East. Sulaiman et al. have reported the results of the Gulf acute HF registry showing that these patients are younger and with a higher prevalence of diabetes and of HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), compared with their Western counterparts.6 Tatari et al.7 have calculated the burden of HF in Lebanon, for which data have not been available so far. They stated that hospitalization care in Lebanon, which is largely delivered by the public sector, yielded direct costs paid by the public and private sector summing up to US$38 million, with an average cost for each HF hospitalization at US$3769. They conclude that the annual total direct cost for HF patients in Lebanon in 2012 was ∼ US$103 million. Hassanein et al.8 report on data from a prospective multicentre observational study of patients presenting to cardiology centres in member countries of the ESC, particularly focusing on 20 centres located all over Egypt. A total of 1475 patients in this registry were hospitalized with acute HF, and the authors concluded that patients in Egypt presented at a much earlier age than those in other regions of the ESC registry. Interesting data have also been published with regard to patients with HF from Japan,9 because Japan has the highest proportion of older people in the world, with 25.9% of the population being 65 years of age or older. The authors report that the number of Japanese outpatients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction was 979 000 in 2014, and there was a projected gradual increase with the ageing of the population. Interestingly, ischaemic aetiology of HF was less frequently observed in Japan than in the Western population. The prevalence of HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), however, was similar between Japan and Western countries. The high overall prevalence of HF not only in the Western world but also in developing countries has led to a number of initiatives such as the workshop organized by the Agenzia Italiana del Farmaco with the aim of discussing unmet needs and ways forward in the development of medicines for HF. This workshop is trying to build a template for meetings devoted to debate of unmet needs with all stakeholders towards producing tentative roadmaps for the future.10 Further action is also needed with respect to risk factors for HF. The role of traditional risk factors for coronary artery disease as well as that of nutrition and lifestyles have been shown by recent analyses.11-15 With the overall increasing number of patients with HF worldwide, new diagnostic and therapeutic avenues are urgently required. Olesen et al.16 recently described the electrocardiogram (ECG) as a first step in the detection of LV systolic dysfunction in the elderly. They used data from 260 patients aged 74–92 years who all had echocardiography, a 12-lead ECG, and natriuretic peptide assessment done. The authors suggested that 90% of LV systolic dysfunction may be detected using an ECG approach. In particular, when there is atrial fibrillation (AF), a paced rhythm, left bundle branch block, a QRS duration of ≥120 ms, or an N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) value >35 pmol/L, a diagnostic echocardiography should be considered. Täger et al.17 studied the cardiac index using data from 50 prospectively included patients with chronic HF and measured cardiac index using both inert gas rebreathing and impedence cardiography at weekly intervals over 3 weeks. The authors concluded than non-invasive measurement of cardiac index was stable over time and in particular that measurement modalities for cardiac index assessment are not interchangeable. The biological variation was less pronounced when inert gas rebreathing techniques were used. In addition to the available prognostic biomarker studies,18-20 prognostic assessments were recently performed in patients with HF using cardiac [123I]metaiodobenzylguanidine imaging and late gadolinium enhancement.21, 22 Kataoka23 investigated the clinical significance of bilateral leg oedema and the added value of monitoring weight gain using data from 1826 outpatient visits of 83 patients with mild to moderate HF. In this study, only 84% of leg oedema events co-existed with weight gain. It was concluded that additional monitoring of weight gain effectively distinguishes clinically significant leg oedema events from insignificant sole leg oedema events. Other studies have shown the prognostic value of the detection of lung congestion through chest X-ray or lung ultrasound in HF patients.24, 25 McDiarmid et al.26 studied the predictive power of late gadolinium enhancement for myocardial recovery in patients with chronic ischaemic HF in 22 patients with severe LV impairment who were randomly assigned to revascularization or not in addition to guideline-indicated pharmacological therapy. They concluded that the duration of the HF syndrome in a given patient is a better predictor of recovery than the transmural extent of late gadolinium enhancement. Acute HF is a life-threatening emergency that requires early diagnosis and treatment.27 Searle et al.28 discussed the differences in the definition of acute HF and the selection criteria for acute HF populations that lead to large differences in the prevalence of acute HF between 1% and 12% of the general population. Cowie et al.29 discussed the variation in the quality of care across hospitals in regions of Europe and the USA. In the call to action paper, they state that in particular in hospital care settings treating patients with acute HF, input from an acute HF expert should be involved to ensure that guidelines and protocols for treatment are implemented for all patients. They also discuss the value of patient education programmes to improve patient outcomes. Access to end-of-life care and support for all patients, family members, and care givers should, in their opinion, form part of a high quality service. Acute HF is a heterogeneous condition with different clinical presentations.30 The variable prevalence of its main clinical manifestation, pulmonary oedema, in clinical trials has been reviewed by Platz et al.31 The role of the different precipitating factors is discussed by Arrigo et al.32 These authors have grouped acute HF patients into the following four groups: acute coronary syndrome, AF, acute pulmonary disease, and other causes. Patients with acute pulmonary disease showed fewer readmission rates but higher 1-year mortality rates, which was especially true in patients 64 years of age or younger. Interesting data were also generated by Sotiropoulos et al.33 who documented—using 402 consecutively hospitalized patients with acute HF—the independent predictive value of an elevated red cell distribution width in patients with HFpEF, but not in those with HFrEF. Konishi et al.34 studied the effects of hypercapnia and hypocapnia among patients with acute HF. Hypercapnia and hypocapnia were observed in 33.7% and 32.6%, respectively, of 193 patients with acute HF. Patients with hypercapnia were more likely to be in New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class IV and to have pulmonary oedema on chest X-ray. The authors of this paper showed that the presence of hypercapnia in acute HF was more frequently associated with immediate airway interventions and possibly involved in the pathophysiology of acute pulmonary oedema. In addition to the effects of gas exchange, Schefold et al.35 showed recently that a single baseline serum creatinine measurement is likewise able to predict death among patients hospitalized for acute HF. Co-morbidities play a major role in disease progression in patients with HF, both among those with HFrEF and among those with HFpEF, however with differences between these two subgroups of HF patients.36, 37 Since no specific treatment is available for HFpEF, the most reasonable approach to symptomatic improvement in patients with HFpEF is treatment of co-morbidities. Skeletal muscle wasting (i.e. sarcopenia) and iron deficiency have recently emerged as important co-morbidities, particularly in patients with HFrEF.38-42 The CONFIRM-HF study aimed to investigate the effects of treating iron deficiency in a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled study using i.v. ferric carboxymaltose to improve 6-min walking distance from baseline to week 24.43 The trial showed good improvement in both quality of life and exercise capacity, and confirmed the overall safety of ferric carboxymaltose in treating iron deficiency in HF.44 A similar randomized and placebo-controlled trial (PRACTICE-ASIA-HF),45 however, conducted as an open-label trial, is aiming to study patients with iron deficiency and a haemoglobin value <14 g/dL. Patients receive either a single dose of 1000 mg of ferric carboxymaltose or i.v. normal saline. Likewise, the primary endpoint of this study is the change in 6-min walk distance within the relatively short time frame of 12 weeks. The results have not been reported so far. The importance of muscle wasting and possible treatment approaches, including exercise training, nutritional support, and medical therapy, were discussed in an overview article by Ebner et al.46 Doehner et al. highlighted the importance of myofibril contractile function of the quadriceps, which is strongly related to insulin sensitivity in patients with chronic HF.47 Frailty, which can be a consequence of muscle wasting, may serve as a new clinical marker for the management of patients with chronic HF, as outlined by Yamada et al.48 Additional insight was provided by Jankowska et al.49 who investigated the prevalence of late-onset hypogonadism in men with systolic HF and its clinical determinants and prognostic consequences. Using data from 201 patients with HFrEF, these authors found that men with HFrEF commonly report sexual complaints and that the combination of sexual dysfunction and testosterone deficiency occurs more frequently than in a general male population. However, the presence of late-onset hypogonadism does not affect long-term mortality when this co-morbidity was adjusted for the severity of HF. Hasin et al. also commented on sexual dysfunction in patients with HF. These authors concluded that sexual dysfunction is prevalent in patients with LV assist device support and that it may be more prominent in these patients than after cardiac transplantation. In addition, they state that ‘problems limiting sexual function related to physiological, psychological, and equipment merit consideration during follow-up’.50 Lastly, Steinbeck et al. have studied a first potential biomarker of skeletal muscle wasting, the C-terminal agrin fragment, in patients with HF.51 Exercise training plays an important part in maintaining patients' quality of life and exercise capacity. However, it is still underused in Europe.52 Nolte et al.53 recently compared the long-term effects of exercise training and exercise capacity, diastolic dysfunction, and quality of life in patients with diastolic dysfunction vs. those with HFpEF using data from 43 patients. These patients performed a combined endurance/resistance training over 6 months on top of usual care. After finishing the study, quality of life as assessed using the Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire, general health perception, and the 9-item patient health questionnaire score only improved in the patients with HFpEF, but not in those with asymptomatic diastolic dysfunction. More encouraging results, however, were found with regard to an increase in the patients' peak VO2 value, which improved significantly both in patients with diastolic dysfunction and in patients with HFpEF. This led the authors to conclude that controlled lifestyle modification with physical activity is effective in both cohorts of patients. Kasner et al.54 identified 52 patients with HFpEF based on their E/e' values. In 27 of 52 patients, E/e' increased during exercise training driven by a failure to augment early diastole. This was correlated with a fall in stroke volume and associated with an increase in diastolic index. Stahrenberg et al.55 performed a cross-sectional analysis from the prospective cohort programme Prevalence and Clinical Course of Diastolic Dysfunction and Heart Failure (DIAST-CHF) that included 1937 patients with at least one risk factor such as hypertension, atherosclerotic disease, diabetes, or obstructive sleep apnoea. They found that the 6-min walk distance was inversely related to E/e' values. In the multivariable analysis, the 6-min walk distance decreased significantly with age, female gender, increasing body mass index, diabetes, COPD, and peripheral artery disease. The authors therefore concluded that classical risk factors for HF and neuroendocrine activation are independently associated with submaximal exercise capacity, whereas diastolic dysfunction obtained at rest is not. The beneficial effects of combined aerobic exercise and inspiratory muscle training vs. aerobic training alone have been shown in a multicentre randomized tral.56 Inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system remains the mainstay of therapy in patients with chronic HF. He et al.57 performed a randomized trial to assess the efficacy and safety of supramaximal titrated inhibition in patients with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy. They concluded that even supramaximal doses of benazepril and valsartan were tolerated and produced extra benefit on top of their low-dose counterparts with regard to clinical outcome and cardiac reverse remodelling.58 PARADIGM-HF is a landmark trial for treatment of HFrEF.59, 60 The success achieved with sacubitril/valsartan vs. enalapril further shows the value of the neurohormonal hypothesis of HF.61 A recent animal model showed that dogs that are randomized to 3 months of oral therapy with ivabradine (compared with no therapy) had a significant decrease of heart rate. The LVEF decreased at 3 months in the control group of HF but increased significantly with ivabradine. Treatment with ivabradine was associated with improved LV diastolic dysfunction, increased sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uptake and ATPase activity, and decreased plasma levels of vasoactive neurohormones, natriuretic peptides, and pro-inflammatory cytokines.62 Subgroup analyses have confirmed the beneficial effects of ivabradine in patients with low blood pressure and diabetes, respectively, in SHIFT.63, 64 Fraccarollo et al.,65 likewise using an animal model, showed that eplerenone as a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist had a superior efficacy as compared with spironolactone during the acute myocardial infarction phase, with more beneficial effects on survival, early cardiac dilatation, and functional decline. Among patients with stable advanced chronic HF, a double-blind placebo-controlled trial was performed allocating patients to an i.v. infusion of placebo or levosimendan in a total of 42 patients. Interestingly, levosimendan treatment significantly improved peak oxygen consumption and reduced the VE/CO2 slope and NT-proBNP level in patients with HF.66 Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a major cause of HF in the peripartum period and is considered potentially life threatening.67 Haghikia et al.68 studied 34 patients with this confirmed diagnosis and undertook cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging at the time of diagnosis and ∼5 months later. About one-third of patients showed LV diastolic dysfunction and right ventricular dysfunction and dilatation, with right ventricular dysfunction being particularly associated with an unfavourable outcome. Most patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy showed a distinct pattern of LV wall motion abnormalities and myocardial scarring. Umazume et al.69 studied changes in blood variables in pregnant women at increased risk of peripartum cardiomyopathy and identified both high sensitive troponin I and NT-proBNP to be highly likely to increase in women with multifoetal pregnancies and/or hypertensive disorders. The authors concluded that the combination of these two biomarkers could contribute to better selection of candidates for echocardiography screening. However, further studies remain necessary.

title: From the Valley of Death to Human-Centric Precision Medicine: The REPO4EU Platform and its Transition into REPOSYSTEM
abstract: Decades of investment in translational medicine have failed to deliver curative therapies for most chronic diseases. 1 The causes are well known: symptom- and organ-based disease definitions, 2,3 animal models with poor predictive validity, 4,5 the scarcity of affordable investigator-initiated trials, 6–8 and a reproducibility crisis in biomedical research. Together, these factors create the “v alley of death” between basic discoveries and clinical benefit. 9 REPO4EU is a Horizon Europe flagship that addresses this crisis by building the first open, pan-European platform for mechanism-based disease re-definition and pairs it—for rapid and safe application—with drug repurposing. At its core lies a multi-agent system powered by applied network medicine 10, AI 11, and mechanistic disease modules 12–14—small, reversible protein–protein interaction dysfunctions that represent the true causal units of disease. This framework allows patient stratification by mechanism, the rational combination of approved drugs, 15 and adaptive Phase IIa/b proof-of-concept trials that are lean, low-cost, and curative rather than symptomatic. The platform already integrates: <!-- named anchor --> Computational tools (Drugst.One DREAM, AI pipelines for module discovery and prioritisation); Preclinical validation in patient-derived cells and organoids, plus genetic disease model phenotyping via INFRAFRONTIER; 12,16–20 Companion diagnostics linked to BBMRI biobanks; Investigator-initiated trial templates (based on REPO-HFPEF, REPO-STROKE, and CIPER), atrial-site database,and new pilot trials(REPO-HYPER, REPO-DIPG, REPO-THYROID). The next step is REPOSYSTEM, a pan-European Research Infrastructure now in preparation to ensure sustainability and scale. REPOSYSTEM will provide a sustainable operations hub—the Brandenburg Institute for Systems Medicine—and integrate seamlessly with existing infrastructures: <!-- named anchor --> INFRAFRONTIER for mechanistic validation in genetic disease models (cellular and animal); BBMRI-ERIC for access to biobanks and diagnostic pipelines; ELIXIR for data standards, FAIRification, and large-scale integration of omics and clinical datasets. This synergy establishes the missing link in the European Research Area: a human-centric precision medicine-enabling ecosystem that moves beyond descriptive, hypothesis-driven “translational medicine” and—in combination with drug repurposing— instead implements a reproducible, mechanistic, and scalable pathway from discovery to rapid cure. REPO4EU demonstrates feasibility and initiates a paradigm shift in medicine. REPOSYSTEM will secure Europe’s global leadership by building the first multinational infrastructure where diseases are defined by mechanisms, diagnostics detect causal dysfunctions, and repurposed drugs restore health. title: The ESC Working Group on Myocardial Function
abstract: The European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Myocardial Function is discussed by its chair, Thomas Thum The 15 Working Groups of the ESC are the scientific backbone of the ESC and have been created to provide their extensive expertise to specific areas of cardiovascular medicine. Together, they contribute to the mission of the ESC: to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease. This year, the Working Groups represent more than 7,100 ESC members, with a growing community of younger members (2,200) under 40 years of age. Education & research are two of the main focus areas of the Working Groups, with the delivery of high-quality educational courses, annual meetings and webinars. As the European references in their fields of expertise, the Working Groups regularly publish papers, consensus documents, handbooks, and journals. They are, without question, a driving force within the ESC. Prof. Cecilia Linde, ESC Vice-President for Working Groups Find out more at https://www.escardio.org/Working-groups online here. As one of the 15 Working Groups of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the Working Group on Myocardial Function (WG MF) is dedicated to the molecular, cellular, and integrative mechanisms underlying cardiac function and dysfunction. The group currently has more than 550 followers, with an active nucleus composed of 10 regular and three ex officio members. It has been my great pleasure and honour to chair the WG since August 2018, with the support of an excellent team, namely vice-chair—Carlo Gabriele Tocchetti (Naples), past-chair—Stéphane Heymans (Maastricht), treasurer—Michele Ciccarelli (Salerno), secretary—Nazha Hamdani (Bochum), and web-editor—Wolfgang Linke (Münster). Members of ESC Working Group on Myocardial Function during group’s Position Paper Meeting, September 2019, Ahrensburg, Germany. (L) to (R): Stéphane Heymans, Jolanda van der Velden, Nazha Hamdani, Carlo Gabriele Tocchetti, Michele Ciccarelli, Dana Dawson, Mauro Giacca, Inês Falcão-Pires, Serena Zacchigna. The aim of the working group is to provide a platform for basic and clinically oriented scientists. Thus, all nucleus members take part in cutting-edge science in their respective institutes, with different focusses and expertise. For instance, Carlo Gabriele Tocchetti, current Director of the Cardio-Oncology Unit in the Department of Translational Medical Sciences, Federico II University, Naples (Italy) contributed to dissect the cardiac contractile effects of nitroxyl (HNO) and the development of a novel HNO donor for treating human heart failure (HF) currently used in clinical trials. The focus of this lab is on post-ischaemic HF, genetic and inflammatory cardiomyopathies, pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction, and HF due to antineoplastic therapies. Michele Ciccarelli (MD, PhD) is an associate professor in Cardiology at the University of Salerno (Italy) working as both clinician and molecular cardiologist. He leads the outpatient clinic for Heart Failure at the University Hospital San Giovanni di Dio e Ruggi. He has expertise in the development and evaluation of animal models of HF, focusing on the multiple roles played by the G protein-coupled receptor kinases. Nazha Hamdani is currently the Head of Department of Molecular and Experimental Cardiology, Ruhr University Bochum (Germany). Her focus is on HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), studying the pathophysiology and especially, mechanisms in inflammatory myocardial disease by providing a link between inflammatory mechanisms to HFpEF. She is principal investigator (PI) in two HFpEF clinical studies. The main scientific interests of Wolfgang Linke, Institut für Physiologie II, Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität Münster (Germany), include basic and translational research on HF and cardiomyopathies, with a focus on cardiomyocyte mechanics, signalling, ultrastructure, and maintenance, including protein quality control. Other current research includes stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte maturation and inherited cardiomyopathies. Jolanda van der Velden, PhD, is chair of the Department for Physiology, Amsterdam University Medical Center, and Director of the Amsterdam Cardiovascular Sciences Institute (The Netherlands). Her main research interest is the role of sarcomere proteins in cardiac performance and especially, in inherited cardiomyopathies. Inês Falcão-Pires has a solid 14-year track-record on animal models of cardiac diseases characterizations and cardiovascular function evaluation. Since 2013, she has been Assistant Professor of Physiology in the Faculty of Medicine of University of Porto (Portugal). A current focus is on the distinct mechanisms between complete and incomplete reverse remodelling in several cardiovascular diseases. Serena Zacchigna (MD, PhD) is active at the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB; Trieste, Italy) where she currently leads the Cardiovascular Biology Laboratory and acts as the Scientific Head of the Bioexperimentation Facility. In 2016, she joined the Medical Department of the University of Trieste. Her research interests focus on the cross-talk between the various cell types residing in the heart during development and disease. She is also an expert in the experimental use of echocardiography and coordinates a study group of clinicians and researchers, aiming at improving the reliability and translational value of this imaging technique. Luc Bertrand is Research Director of the Fonds National de la Recherche Scientifique (Belgium) and Full Professor in Biochemistry in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of Louvain (Brussels). He is co-director of the pole of Cardiovascular Research (IREC Institute). His research group aims to understand the relationship between metabolism, post-translational modifications and cardiac (dys)functions in cardiac hypertrophy, HF, or diabetic cardiomyopathy. Amongst other discoveries, Luc Bertrand recently established AMP-activated protein kinase as a putative therapeutic target to prevent cardiac hypertrophy development by targeting protein O-GlcNAcylation. Stéphane Heymans, past-chair of the WG MF, is currently active at the Department of Cardiology, Maastricht University Medical Centre, Center for Heart Failure Research, Cardiovascular Research Institute Maastricht (CARIM), University Hospital Maastricht (The Netherlands) and focuses on inflammatory and genetic cardiomyopathies. He is current chair of the Basic Science section of the HFA. My own focus is on non-coding RNAs as key regulators in cardiovascular biology and HF. Identification of new therapeutic options and further aspects in translational cardiovascular medicine, including large animal and early clinical trial studies, are pursued in my Institute for Molecular and Translational Therapeutic Strategies at the Hannover Medical School (Germany), which currently consists of about 50 persons. Together with Cardior Pharmaceuticals GmbH, a spin-off of Hannover Medical School, we have developed innovative ncRNA-based treatment strategies to a world-wide first clinical trial using ncRNA blockers in patients with HF. The nucleus of the WG MF has appointed three ex officio members, who provide their respective expertise on myocardial function in cardiomyopathies, metabolic disorders, and as a function of physical exercise (Dana Dawson, Aberdeen), OMICS technologies and bioinformatics (Manuel Mayr, London), and cardiac regeneration (Mauro Giacca, London). The Giacca laboratory at King’s College London has a main interest in developing innovative therapeutics for cardiac protection and repair. By high throughput screenings, the laboratory has identified a few microRNAs that promote cardiac regeneration through the simulation of endogenous cardiomyocyte proliferation. Dana Dawson leads a clinical and preclinical research group at the University of Aberdeen as well as being an active member of the National Health Service Acute Cardiology service at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary. This allows her to bring a translational approach to the Working Group, from the eyes of a clinical scientist with clinical vision. Manuel Mayr, in addition to his scientific achievements in the development of innovative cardiac biomarkers, is active in educational workshops for WG members, for instance in the context of the HFA Winter Meeting which is traditionally held every year in Les Diablerets, Switzerland. Beside the individual scientific publications of the WG and especially, the nucleus members, the WG MF has also a high output of position papers. As a matter of fact, the traditional biennial meetings held since 2009 in Varenna are the highlights within the WG MF’s activities. Mostly held as joint meetings together with the ESC WG on Cellular Biology of the Heart (WG CB) the ‘Varenna’ meetings aim to bring together outstanding scientific speakers, key opinion leaders, and young investigators in a stimulating atmosphere that creates moments of inspiring scientific exchange and discussion. In 2019, the meeting was held for the first time in the city of Naples, organized by Rosalinda Madonna (chairperson of the WG CB) and me. Entitled ‘Bench to Bedside 4.0 – new therapeutic entry points to fight cardiovascular disease’, the meeting underlined once more the strong translational attitude of the WG MF. With more than 150 active participants, the meeting was so far the largest event of the Working Group and a great success, which will hopefully have a worthy successor next year in 2021. I conclude expressing my hope that the ESC Working Group on Myocardial Function may continue to thrive and prosper! Stay connected to any news of the WG MF or become a member via https://www.escardio.org/Working-groups/Working-Group-on-Myocardial-Function/About. I thank Sabine Kafert-Kasting, project manager in my institute, for help with the manuscript. Conflict of interest: T.T. filed and licensed patents in the field of non-coding RNAs. He is founder and shareholder of Cardior Pharmaceuticals GmbH, a clinical-stage biotech company.

title: Proteinopathy: Shared Feature Between the Heart and Brain in Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: “I put my heart and my soul into my work, and have lost my mind in the process.” Vincent Van Gogh ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE BURDEN AND CLINICAL PATHOGENESIS Alzheimer's disease (AD) comprises around 70% of all dementia cases and is the leading cause of death among neurological diseases. Over the last 30 years, the burden of AD has substantially increased across the globe. Between 2010 and 2020, worldwide fatalities from AD and dementia showed a 44% rise, surpassing the 21% increase in deaths related to heart disease. The United States burden of AD and related dementias is projected to double by 2050, during which around 13 million individuals are expected to suffer from AD.1 Although aging is a primary risk factor, it is also possible to experience an early onset of AD.2 The progression of the disease starts from preclinical stages and advances toward mild cognitive impairment, eventually leading to AD dementia. Detecting the disease in its early stages remains a challenge as clinical symptoms tend to appear years later. This gradual and debilitating pattern of AD causes a significant financial and human burden. One of the main focuses of extensive research on AD is the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tau tangles in the brain, which is considered to be a hallmark in the development of the disease. Recently, the FDA granted accelerated approval to the Aβ-directed monoclonal antibody lecanemab that prevents its deposition to treat AD.3 ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE AND CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH Numerous epidemiological studies have explored the link between cardiovascular diseases and AD. Evidence suggests that older individuals with cardiovascular disease are at a high risk of developing AD.4,5 This interrelationship is reinforced by the fact that both conditions share similar risk factors and genetic profiles such as hypertension, hypercholesteremia, obesity, and APOE polymorphisms. Additionally, alterations in vascular and perfusion mechanisms may contribute to the development of AD because individuals with AD often exhibit a decrease in cerebral blood flow.6 Chronic hypoperfusion causes oxidative stress and neuronal death.7 Over time, energy depletion may trigger development of Aβ plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. However, this remains a putative mechanism in the absence of clinical proof. Approaching the brain–heart interaction from a different perspective, AD may be linked to cardiac pathologies (Fig. 1). Cohort studies have revealed an association between AD and diastolic dysfunction.8–10 Additionally, the degree of cognitive impairment seems to be related to the severity of diastolic dysfunction. It is natural for cardiac and cognitive functions to decline with age. In a retrospective cross-sectional study, Troncone et al11 compared 22 patients with AD to 35 age-matched control subjects and found that those with AD experienced diastolic dysfunction at a younger age. Interestingly, only old AD patients exhibited significant cardiac hypertrophy along with decreased aortic valve compliance. These observations suggest the possibility that cardiac hypertrophy is not solely a cardiovascular event and point toward new prospects for understanding AD-associated cardiac pathogenesis.FIGURE 1.: The intricate association between AD and diastolic dysfunction. The 2 conditions share common risk factors and histopathological accumulation of amyloid-β and tau protein (created using BioRender.com).Recent experiments using the 5XFAD mouse as a model of AD provided evidence for the possible involvement of metabolic derangement in AD pathogenesis and associated cardiac dysfunction.12 At 6 months of age, 5XFAD mice show signs of cardiac systolic dysfunction and reduced calcium influx. The study also found evidence of energy depletion, such as increased AMPK phosphorylation in the brain, and impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and pyruvate dehydrogenase enzymatic activity in both the brain and the left ventricle. This was accompanied by an increase in oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators. Although it is widely accepted that dysregulation in mitochondrial homeostasis has a significant impact on cardiac contractility,13 the root cause of this phenomenon in AD remains unclear. PROTEINOPATHIES IN THE HEART OF ALZHEIMER'S The current prevailing knowledge and a primary focus in addressing AD is centered around understanding and preventing buildup of Aβ peptides and neurofibrillary tangles formed by tau proteins in the brain. Aβ is generated by the proteolytic processing of amyloid precursor protein by β and γ secretases. The γ secretase's catalytic subunit comprises PSEN1 and PSEN2, highly conserved polytopic membrane proteins known as presenilins. Early familial AD is identified by genetic mutations in amyloid precursor protein, PSEN1, or PSEN2 leading to excessive production of Aβ. However, late-onset sporadic AD is associated with the APOE gene, particularly the APOE4 allele, which prevents the elimination of Aβ. Although proteotoxicity is well-recognized in AD, several investigations have shown the involvement of disrupted proteostasis in cardiovascular diseases such as idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.14 Similar amyloid aggregate deposits and common and novel genetic variants were identified.15,16 Mechanistically, genetic mutations in presenilins are believed to affect the expression of excitation–contraction coupling proteins resulting in impaired calcium homeostasis and cardiomyocyte dysfunction.15 Oligomeric aggregates were also shown to provoke a cellular response. Research studies on HFpEF have identified various preclinical models, including the 2-hit model and ZSF1-Ob rats. These models have demonstrated that an "inappropriate" protein unfolding response because of endoplasmic reticulum stress contributes to the development of diastolic dysfunction.17 Despite this, protein folding has yet to be thoroughly investigated in cases of HFpEF in humans. Recently, epidemiological studies unveiled a high prevalence of structural and functional cardiac abnormalities in patients with AD.18,19 Misfolded proteins were also found accumulated in the heart of AD patients. Troncone et al11 reported a significant increase in Aβ-40 and Aβ-42 aggregates in the brain and heart tissues of selective AD patients maintained on respiratory support. Notably, diastolic dysfunction phenotype again prevailed in AD patients starting at early ages. The isolation of cardiomyocytes from an old AD patient displayed impaired Ca2+ homeostasis characterized by reduced velocities of relaxation and prolonged Ca2+ transients. Although limited in the number of patients, it seems plausible for an insult provoked by the accumulation of Aβ in cardiomyocytes to underlie the functional defect. It is now accepted that Aβ deposition is not uniquely featured in the brain in the context of AD. However, it is still unclear whether this mechanism could be described as a common, systemic, or metastatic pathogenesis. Neurofibrillary tangles are another prominent pathological lesion of AD formed by the intracellular accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins. Being a scaffolding protein, tau binds and maintains the stability of microtubules. Hyperphosphorylation of tau causes its disassembly from microtubules into filamentous aggregates. A strong correlation was demonstrated between NTFs and neurodegeneration in synaptic dysfunction and neuronal loss.20 At first, tau expression was considered brain-specific. However, a recent study by Luciana et al revealed increased phosphorylation of a high-molecular-weight isoform of tau in idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and in the heart of AD patients as in the brain.21 In failing hearts, microtubule structure and dynamics are crucial. The detyrosination of microtubules can affect compliance during diastole by increasing viscoelasticity and myocardial stiffness.22 In a humanized tau mouse model of AD, cardiac diastolic function progressively deteriorated concomitantly with tau accumulation.21 Tau oligomers were shown localized in the cardiomyocytes that displayed loss of tyrosinated tubules and impaired relaxation. Therefore, tauopathy is likely involved, at least in part, in diastolic dysfunction. THERAPEUTIC APPROACHES FOR ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE Initially, the main objective in devising disease-modifying drugs for AD was reducing the presence of Aβ plaques in the brain. Numerous compounds were tested to regulate Aβ levels by minimizing its formation, preventing its clumping, or promoting its elimination. In animal studies, targeting Aβ has been successful in ameliorating cognitive performance, but when applied to AD patients, these attempts were hindered or terminated because of issues with treatment effectiveness, dosage, disease phase, length of therapy, or toxicity.23 Notably, lecanemab only moderately slows cognitive and functional decline in early-stage AD cases. As a result, researchers have shifted their focus to targeting tau pathology, which has been shown to strongly correlate with cognitive status. Aβ was thought to act upstream of tau; however, the latter seems to be independent. Preclinical studies have shown that anti-tau immunotherapy and liposome-based vaccines could be a promising new approach in AD.24–26 Despite numerous trials over the years, only FDA-approved drugs that regulate neurotransmitters have been effective, such as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like galantamine, donepezil, and rivastigmine, and N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antagonist, memantine, which works by targeting the glutamatergic system.27,28 Building on the heart–head connection, experts have also recognized that antihypertensive treatments such as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin type 1 receptor blockers, and potassium-sparing diuretics have a protective effect against AD.29 Additionally, targeting the ApoE gene, which is linked to both coronary heart disease and AD and is known to cause hypercholesteremia, has shown promise in reducing protein buildup and neurodegeneration in animal models of AD.30 To better understand and manage the complex development of cognitive impairment in heart failure, it is crucial to conduct trials that explore the effects of diastolic dysfunction treatments on cognitive function. One potential solution in comanaging AD and cardiovascular disease could be repurposing drugs (Table 1). Additionally, future therapeutic strategies targeting protein misfolding need to consider the presence of proteinopathies in the heart of AD. TABLE 1. - Possibly Beneficial Therapies for Both AD and Cardiovascular Disease Search Term Apoptosis Embelin and esculetin ER stress NA Inflammasome Inflammasome inhibitors and flavonoids Metabolic syndrome PPARα agonists, GLP-1 (receptor agonist), triple G agonists, metformin, and flavonoids Mitochondrial dysfunction NA Oxidative stress Curcumin nanoparticles Proteinopathy ACMs and curcumin nanoparticles Vascular inflammation/dysfunction ACEIs and ARBs Current/future drugs were identified by searching PubMed (January 1, 2021 to March 10, 2023) with the following terms: Alzheimer's AND cardiovascular disease AND drug AND [search term].ACEI, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor; ACM, constrained peptides mimicking the Aβ amyloid core; ARB, angiotensin type 1 receptor blocker; NA, none available. CONCLUSIONS Although limited, present evidence highlights a systemic feature of AD that exacerbates the burden on our aging population, namely proteinopathy. There is need for advances in well-targeted therapies. For optimal intervention, therapeutics in clinical trials against AD controlling protein misfolding are encouraged to explore outcomes on the heart and the brain in combination. Proteinopathies could possibly be as well a novel therapeutic target in HFpEF, for which diastolic dysfunction is a cardinal feature and is common in the elderly.

title: Figures of the Heart Failure Association (HFA): Prof. Dr. med. Thomas Thum, Chair of the ESC Working Group on Myocardial Function and Ex-Officio HFA Board Member (2018–2020)
abstract: Thomas Thum has recently joined the Board of the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC); he is the current Chair of the ESC Working Group on Myocardial Function. As such he has just organized, together with the Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart, the Biennial Joint Meeting of both Working Groups, this year for the first time in the city of Naples, dedicated to ‘Bench to Bedside 4.0 - New therapeutic entry points to fight cardiovascular disease’. The meeting was supported by the HFA and two sessions were provided by the Heart Failure Specialists of Tomorrow and the Scientists of Tomorrow, respectively, and proved to contribute to the great success of the meeting. Thomas' further commitment to the ESC includes his activity as an Editorial Board member of Cardiovascular Research. Thomas Thum studied medicine in Hannover, with state examination and medical thesis in 2001 and board examination for internal medicine/cardiology in 2009/2010. He received his PhD at the Imperial College, London, UK (2008). Thomas pursued his clinical and postdoctoral training in Hannover and Würzburg and became Research Junior Group Leader ‘Cardiac Wounding and Healing’ at the Interdisciplinary Center for Clinical Research (IZKF) of the Julius-Maximilians University, Würzburg (Germany) from 2006 to 2009. Since October 2009 he is a full professor in permanent position at the Hannover Medical School (MHH), and Director of the Institute of Molecular and Translational Therapeutic Strategies (IMTTS; http://www.mh-hannover.de/imtts.html). Since July 2013 he is also Visiting Professor at the National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London, UK. Prof. Thum is Fellow of the American Heart Association, of the ESC, and of the HFA. Furthermore, he is member of the German Society of Cardiology (DGK), the German Society of Internal Medicine (DGIM), and member ‘at large’ of the World Section of the International Society for Heart Research (ISHR). Thomas is a substitute member of the Management Committee of the European COST Action CardioRNA (to represent Germany), and participates in the DFG-funded Cluster of Excellence REBIRTH (From REgenerative BIology to Reconstructive THerapies) in Hannover since 2006; he is elected spokesman of the initiative since December, 2018. Thomas Thum is also active at the Hannover Medical School as vice-chair of the PhD Program ‘Molecular Medicine’ of the Hannover Biomedical Research School, vice-chair on Internationalization, and member of the steering committee of the Hannover Unified Biobank (HUB). Thomas' main scientific interest is in the role of non-coding RNAs in cardiovascular biology and disease, mechanisms of development and treatment of heart failure (HF), and diverse aspects in translational cardiovascular medicine, including large animal and early clinical trial studies. Thus Thomas (co-) authors >300 publications in peer-reviewed journals (H-index 65; m-index 3.4) and received a large number of important public grants so far, including but not limited to a project within the DFG-funded Clinical Research Group (KFO) 311 ‘(Pre-) terminal heart and lung failure - mechanical unloading and repair’ at MHH, the MIRVAD grant of the Leducq foundation (Leducq Trans-Atlantic Network and Training Program on MicroRNA-Based Therapeutic Strategies in Vascular Disease, 2014–2019), for which he is the network coordinator, and an ERC Consolidator Grant to explore selected long non-coding RNAs as diagnostics and therapeutic targets for HF (LONGHEART, 2015–2020). His group is also successful in EU consortium projects such as FIBROTARGETS (2013–2017), HOMAGE (2013–2019), and CARDIOREGENIX (2019–2023). His work has contributed to many ground-breaking papers, a very few of which are listed below.1-8 Prof. Thum received a number of honourable awards such as the Hugo-Geiger Award of the Bavarian Ministry of Science, Germany (2001), the Parmley Award of the American College of Cardiology (2005), the Oskar-Lapp Award (2008), the Albert-Fraenkel Award (2010) and the Franz-Maximilian-Groedel Award (2012) of the German Cardiac Society, the Outstanding Achievement Award of the ESC (2011), and the Outstanding Investigator Award of the ISHR (2015), to mention a few. Based on his broad experience and expertise, Thomas Thum acts as a reviewer for the European Research Council (ERC) and for a number of national institutions in Germany, UK, France, Ireland, Austria, and the Netherlands, as well as Advisory Board Member or Member of a pool of experts, e.g. in the National Medical Research Council, Singapore (2014–2018), the Pasteur Institute, Lille, France (since 2016), the Aachen Interdisciplinary Center for Clinical Research (IZKF), University Aachen, Germany (since 2016), and the German National Committee for the Protection of Laboratory Animals, German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (since 2018). He is Consulting Editor at Circulation Research, International Associate Editor at the European Heart Journal, and Editorial Board Member at Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology; Basic Research in Cardiology; the American Journal of Physiology – Heart and Circulatory Physiology, PLoS One, and Physiol Genomics. Last but not least, Thomas Thum is a successful entrepreneur and patent holder, with > 30 filed and partly granted patents (nine of them licensed), and founder of the clinical stage biotech company Cardior Pharmaceuticals GmbH (www.cardior.de). T: Current clinical practice is dominated by very common treatments of HF patients with some progress in HF with reduced ejection fraction and little progress in HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) so far. Fur sure we need a much better stratification of HF patients finally to design new therapeutic entry points, e.g. with respect to co-morbidities. For instance, HFpEF patients with cardiac dysfunction due to enhanced cardiac fibrosis9 may need different treatment approaches compared to HFpEF patients with diabetic10, 11 and/or kidney co-morbidities.12 Through emerging new technologies such as RNA and single-cell sequencing, we may be able in the future to identify new patient cohorts/subgroups that will benefit better from a treatment approach than others do. The great new HFA initiative, the ESC HFA Atlas in Europe, will also help here a lot in the future. Additionally, there will be much more preclinical research in HF models with co-morbidities. This may allow us to identify so far unknown targets and pathways either in heart tissue directly or somewhere else, whose targeting will lead to better efficacy of HF therapy. T: One of the big challenges I see is how to bring more new therapeutic molecules into clinical development. Currently, there is a big gap between basic science and finally testing new upcoming molecules/mechanisms in the clinic. There are many obvious reasons for this, such as lack of entrepreneurship and industry cooperation, limited knowledge and limited translational funding opportunities. For this we need to work hard to implement better strategies how Academia and Industry will efficiently join forces in the development of optimized therapeutic and diagnostic strategies. In addition we need more public/governmental support for translational development of targets into early clinical testing. This topic is one of the aims I will work on during my time being a member of the HFA Board. T: One important point would be to continue both the support of young clinicians and basic scientists. In addition, we need to further create an environment boosting joint research between clinicians, translational, basic scientists and the Industry. To invest in the young as well as in joint European research strategies will allow sustainability of our HFA and guarantee continuous success. T: It's a great field in dire need to find novel targets and approaches and thus a great area and opportunity for young clinicians/researchers. Depending on the career stage, different things should be taken into consideration. At an early stage I think it is important to find a group that either scientifically and/or clinically is very active and belongs to the best. It is also important that you try to publish in the best journals and seek for grant support as soon as possible; this may include travel grants in the beginning and more sophisticated project grants at a later stage. Currently, there are many great European funding opportunities also for PhD students to even work part-time in various different labs including that from Pharmaceutical Industry. Such a broad perspective will widen your horizon and prepare you to become a next-generation leader in HF and hopefully also in the HFA. T: There have been (fortunately) a number of different great mentors in my career. I had very personal memorable meetings with Prof. Philip Poole-Wilson, who was my mentor during my PhD thesis at the Imperial College in London. He really took his time to show me a lot of skills in scientific writing and thinking, which helped me a lot in my future career. As time is one of the scarce resources we as clinicians and scientists have, it's wonderful to spend some of that rare resource also to building the career of others. I adopted this strategy with great experiences and memories. Andrew J.S. Coats University of Warwick, UK and IRCCS San Raffaele Pisana, Rome, Italy [email protected]

title: An Unexpected Ally in Heart Failure Treatment: Unlocking the Potential of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors Across Patient Subpopulations
abstract: Heart failure (HF), a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, globally affects millions of people. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), originally developed as antihyperglycaemic drugs, have shown broad therapeutic efficacy in managing HF across the spectrum of ejection fractions. Recent research explored evidence on efficacy and safety of SGLT2i across HF subtypes, focusing on their mechanisms, clinical benefits and implications for future HF management. SGLT2i, including dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, work by decreasing glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule, promoting glucosuria and mild osmotic diuresis. This mechanism contributes to improved glycaemic control and a lower body weight. Importantly, the beneficial effects of SGLT2i on HF are irrespective of diabetes mellitus or other co-morbidities, with robust results on mortality, HF hospitalisations and renal function.1, 2 Real-world nationwide data in >50 000 patients from the Swedish HF population confirmed the compelling evidence from the randomized trials that patients with HF who receive SGLT2i were at significant lower risk for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and HF and all-cause readmissions. The results were consistent in the overall and diabetes cohorts. The effect size was greater than in randomized trials.3 Different explanations may be valid, as the event rates are often much higher in real-world than those reported in the randomized trials, the latter including more stable HF patients with fewer or less severe co-morbidities. Not only is the efficacy of SGLT2i well-established, but their use has furthermore proven to be safe. A large contemporary meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials with over 20 000 participants could not only show reduced mortality but also show reduced severe adverse events. The effect was more prominent in patients with reduced ejection fraction and patients taking dapagliflozin. Next, renal events were reduced, and there were no discontinuations due to major hypoglycaemia, ketoacidosis or adverse limb events. However, the risk of genitourinary infections and volume depletion was higher compared with placebo, emphasizing the need for thorough patient education when initiating SGLT2i therapy.4 It remains an open question as to whether all SGLT2i are equally effective for the treatment of HF. Head-to-head comparisons of SGLT2i treatments in HF are lacking. A network meta-analysis based on a Bayesian statistical approach revealed no significant difference among different SGLT2i treatments for the composite outcomes and individual clinical endpoints in patients with HF. By ranking probability, sotagliflozin had the lowest risk of the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, whereas dapagliflozin had the lowest risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular death, regardless of ejection fraction.5 Another meta-analysis revealed dapagliflozin to have a stronger protective effect in preventing mortality without a significant difference in serious adverse events.4 The results should be interpreted with caution because of the heterogeneity between the included randomized clinical trials and other sources of potential biases. Another area that requires further clarification is the precise mechanism by which these drugs exert their effects. Cardiac remodelling in HF involves structural and functional myocardial changes, typically fibrosis, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and shifts in cellular composition and metabolics, leading to reduced cardiac function and disease progression.6-8 Meanwhile, the effects of SGLT2i extend beyond glycemic control and diuresis by promoting glucosuria. Mechanistic studies of cardiac remodelling demonstrated that SGLT2i intake induces regression of left ventricular mass in patients with type 2 diabetes or coronary artery disease, as shown by Verma et al. in the EMPA-HEART CardioLink-6 trial.9 Substudies of this randomized trial with empagliflozin suggest that SGLT2i mitigate modulation of inflammatory and profibrotic responses. Patients with an elevated baseline neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 7 levels exhibit a significantly higher left ventricular mass, but empagliflozin treatment was consistently beneficial on LV reverse remodelling irrespective of these marker levels.10, 11 Moreover, the reduction in left ventricular mass was irrespective of the duration of diabetes.12 These findings must be interpreted with consideration of small sample sizes and post hoc exploratory study designs. Nevertheless, they make us curious about the pivotal effects SGLT2i might have in cardiac remodelling. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is one of the most common co-morbidities that increase morbidity and mortality in HF.13 A meta-analysis by Kato et al. showed that the beneficial effect of SGLT2i is similar in HF patients with and without CKD.14 There are also reports on the use of SGLT2i in patients with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis, demonstrating that, when used together with sacubitril/valsartan, it is both effective and safe.15 The mechanism of action of SGLT2i through proximal renal tubules may also affect kidney health. In cases of acute decompensated HF, empagliflozin caused significant reduction in markers of tubular kidney damage within just 3 days of use. A potential mechanism of this renoprotective effect is a regional haemodynamic change of at the kidney level, leading to reduced glomerular filtration pressure without altering systemic general haemodynamic parameters, such as cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance index.16 However, Dai et al. demonstrated in an animal model that dapagliflozin reduced infiltration, fibrosis, and maladaptive remodelling of the right atrium and pulmonary arteries, lowering the risk of right heart dysfunction and indirectly susceptibility to atrial fibrillation.17 This mechanism may be significantly beneficial in patients with advanced HF who are candidates for heart transplantation, as it helps maintain low pulmonary vascular resistance, a known risk factor for right ventricular failure of the graft.18 This also applies to less-studied causes of HF, such as congenital heart disease. Egorova et al. used SGLT2i in patients with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries and a systemic right ventricle, who could not tolerate sacubitril/valsartan. Treatment with SGLT2i resulted in less HF hospitalizations and improvements in functional and echocardiographic status.19 Although there is ample evidence for conventional HF medications, the role of the four pillars of HF therapy in different HF subpopulations remains to be fully elucidated. Strict inclusion criteria often exclude complex patient populations from randomized trials. For example, in patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, therapeutic response on angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and beta blockers seems to be different from other patients with HF.20 Therefore, neurohormonal blockers are currently not widely prescribed and often discontinued in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy.21 Initiation of dapagliflozin seemed to be well tolerated in patients with tafamidis-treated transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy. Observational data indicate potential improvement in biomarker levels, suggesting a role in disease stabilization.22 However, patient groups were small and the study was retrospective. Moreover, mouse models could not show a benefit for dapagliflozin in the progression of heart failure, cardiac inflammation and pathological changes in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy.23 Collaborative prospective trials to expand sample sizes are highly needed. Reports on the cost-effectiveness of using SGLT2i across the spectrum of HF are also noteworthy. Tang et al. assessed the utility of dapagliflozin in HFpEF/HFmrEF from the perspective of the Chinese public healthcare system, demonstrating its effectiveness based on the total cost, quality-adjusted life-years per patient, and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio.24 Similarly, Tsutsui et al. demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of empagliflozin in HFpEF in Japan.25 Extending this analysis to European countries, Kolovos et al. confirmed that empagliflozin is both clinically and cost-effective for patients with HFpEF/HFmrEF, supporting its use across diverse healthcare environments.26 In summary, SGLT2i have transformed to a foundational pillar of HF treatment over the recent years, offering therapeutic benefits across the HF spectrum regardless of diabetic status. Research suggested multifactorial mechanisms of action, encompassing among others glycaemic control, increased diuresis, blood pressure reduction, renal protection and cardiac remodelling by modulation of inflammatory and profibrotic pathways. SGLT2i deservedly earned their position as a class I recommendation for HF. With ongoing studies and real-world data supporting their broad utility and safety, clinicians and researchers will continue to optimize their use to tackle the persistent challenges in HF management. abstract: PS089 Pathophysiological and Therapeutic Implications of Urocortin-2 in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction Inês Vasconcelos1,2,3, Pedro Vaz-Salvador1, Rui Adão1, Glória Conceição1, Daniela Miranda-Silva1, Joana Santos-Gomes1, Beatriz Rego1, Carolina Maia-Rocha1, Pedro Mendes-Ferreira1, Adelino Ferreira Leite-Moreira1, Ana Patrícia Fontes-Sousa3, Carmen Brás-Silva1,4 1Department of Surgery and Physiology, Cardiovascular Research and Development Center -UnIC, Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal,2Faculty of Sciences, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal,3School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (ICBAS), University of Porto, Porto, Portugal,4Faculty of Nutrition and Food Sciences, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal Introduction: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for a rising proportion of heart failure cases with mortality rates of 29% at 1-year and 65% at 5-years [1]. Current treatment options are limited and aim only for symptomatic relief [2]. Urocortin-2 (Ucn-2) belongs to the corticotro- phin-releasing hormone family and has been found to have significant beneficial hemodynamic, hormonal and renoprotective effects both in animal models and humans with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction [3–6]. Aim: In this work we studied the role of the Ucn-2/CRHR2 system in the pathophysiology of HFpEF and evaluated the efficacy of Ucn-2 as a novel therapeutic strategy for this disease. Methods: 18-week-old male ZSF1-Lean (n = 26) and ZSF1- Obese (n = 28) rats randomly received either Ucn-2 (15 μg/kg/day, subcutaneously) or vehicle (0.9% NaCl) for 12 weeks. During the treatment period, evolution of cardiac (dys)function was assessed by echocardiography and exercise testing. After treatment, invasive hemodynamic analysis was performed, with subsequent sample collection. Results: mRNA expression of Ucn-2 and CRHR2 was decreased in the left ventricle (LV) of ZSF1-Obese rats compared to ZSF1-Lean and correlated with LV structure and diastolic function. We found that ZSF1- Obese animals display increased LV end-diastolic pressure, end-systolic pressure, and tau compared to ZSF1-Lean animals. Ucn-2 treatment significantly decreased all these parameters. Chronic treatment did not have any effect on body weight gain, exercise capacity or fasting blood glucose levels, but cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area was increased in Obese rats and attenuated by Ucn-2 treatment. Similarly, we found that Ucn-2 therapy attenuated LV mass, measured through echocardiography, in ZSF1-Obese rats compared to the non-treated group. Conclusion: This work suggests that the Ucn-2/CRHR2 system is altered in experimental HFpEF and that chronic administration of Ucn-2 attenuates LV remodeling, in particular the hypertrophic changes of the cardiac muscle. Parallel Oral Session - Internal Medicine PS099 Co-Infection by DNA Viruses in Patients after Kidney Transplantation Saaz Sahani1, Miroslav Fajfr2 1Charles University in Prague,2Department of Clinical Microbiology, Faculty Hospital in Hradec Kralove Introduction: Post-transplant immunosuppressive therapy may give rise to both opportunistic infections and reactivation of latent viruses. Polyomaviruses (JCPyV and BKPyV) and cytomegalovirus (hCMV) are such latent pathogens that affect recipient outcomes after allogenic kidney transplantation. Polyomavirus associated nephropathy (PVAN) is a serious allograft reaction that resembles acute rejection. It has been found that infection with two or more viruses has a greater impact on kidney graft function than a single infection. Aim: The main aim of the project was to investigate DNA virus co-infections in post-renal transplant patients and their impact on clinical outcomes. Methods: The study consisted of a total of 180 patients (120 recipients and 60 donors). Consecutive blood and urine samples were collected 1-year post-transplantation (between 2017 and 2020). BKPyV positive patients were isolated and subsequently screened for the presence of hCMV and JCPyV. PCR was performed via the RotorGene instrument. Patients reported with co-infections were evaluated for clinical outcomes. Results: 36 patients developed BKPyV positivity during the first year after kidney transplantation. 3 patients expressed co-infection by BKPyV and JCPyV and 3 patients with co-infec- tion by BKPyV and hCMV. Significant enhancement of BKPyV copy numbers were noted in BKPyV-JCPyV co-infections. 1 of 5 cases of Polyomavirus-associated nephropathy was associated with a co-infection (BKPyV+JCPyV coinfection). However, long term graft survival was not affected. Conclusion: Polyomavirus-associated nephropathy (PVAN) incidence has increased by 10% in the past decade, often leading to graft loss. BKPyV reactivation is possibly enhanced by JCPyV infection, making these co-infected recipients an important risk collective. There are currently no antiviral treatments for Polyomaviruses and reduction of the immunosuppressant regimen poses threats to both graft and recipient. This highlights the importance of donor screening and risk-stratification based on serology. Poster Session - Public Health & Medical Informatics PS113 Development of an Application for Analyzing Glycemic Variability in People With Diabetes Who use an Intermittently Scanned Continuous Glucose Monitoring System Bruno Soares1, Sofia Teixeira2, Maria Helena Cardoso2 1lnstitute of Biomedical Sciences Abel Salazar (ICBAS), University of Porto, Porto, Portugal, 2Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, Department of Medicine, Centro Hospitalar e Universitário do Porto, Porto, Portugal Introduction: Glycemic variability is a problem in the management of diabetes, contemplating patterns of hyper and hy- poglycemia.[1] With the definition of metrics useful to clinical practice for continuous glucose monitoring data[2], the need to overcome the shortcomings of existing applications/softwares urges. Aim: This project aims to develop and validate an application that processes data from intermittently scanned continuous glucose monitoring, calculating the metrics and verifying the usefulness of linear interpolation and the Glucose Management Indicators formulae, comparing the latter with glycated hemoglobin. Methods: The study's first step was to develop two versions of an application (with and without interpolation), using VBA in an Excel sheet; the second to confirm its validity, assessed through the comparison of the metrics obtained by both new versions with the manufacturer program and with glycated hemoglobin, using Pearson and Intraclass correlation coefficients and the standardized differences[3]. Forty eight raw data files and the equivalent PDF were downloaded from forty four type-1 diabetic patients of the Endocrinology Department of Porto's University Hospital. Results: The metrics calculated by both new versions and the manufacturer program showed great correlation and agreement - these were higher between the without interpolation version and the manufacturer program. The only relevant (>10%) standardized differences were on the Glucose Management Indicators. When comparing Glucose Management Indicators with glycated hemoglobin, the standardized difference was lowest for the without interpolation version (17.35%) and highest for the manufacturer program (30.33%). Conclusion: The developed application is updated to the most recent metrics, validated in a type 1 diabetic population and an excellent tool for clinical practice and research promotion, due to not requiring internet connection or previous installation. The results suggest that interpolation may introduce an element of confounding. However, further studies are needed. Bergenstal's formula[4] used in the new application, is closer to glycated hemoglobin than Nathan's formula[5], used in the manufacturer program. References 1. Klonoff DC, Ahn D, Drincic A. Parallel Oral Session - Oncology & Molecular Biology PS131 Deciphering the Role of Vitamin D in Early Lung Development Inês Caldeira1’2, Jorge Correia-Pinto1,2,3, Rute S Moura1,2 1Life and Health Sciences Research Institute (ICVS), School of Medicine, University of Minho, 4710-057 Braga, Portugal,2ICVS/3B's - PT Government Associate Laboratory, 4710- O57Braga/Guimarães, Portugal, Department of Pediatric Surgery, Hospital of Braga, 4710-243 Braga, Portugal Introduction: The high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency is now considered a public health concern, affecting people of all ages worldwide, particularly childbearing women and children. There is an association between maternal vitamin D deficiency and various adverse maternal-fetal health outcomes, including abnormal fetal growth and development. Regarding the developing lung, it is recognized that vitamin D is crucial for later stages of lung development, specifically for lung maturation processes, thus influencing the respiratory health of the offspring. Nevertheless, little is known about its role in pulmonary branching in the early stages of development. Aim: This work aims to unravel the regulatory role of vitamin D during branching morphogenesis, using the chicken embryo as a model. Methods: The expression pattern of the vitamin D processing machinery was characterized by in situ hybridization (ISH) in b1, b2, and b3 embryonic chick lungs (one, two, or three secondary bronchi, respectively). To assess the impact of vitamin D on lung growth, in vitro lung explants were cultured in increasing doses of 1,25(OH)2D3 or DMSO (control) for 48 hours and analyzed morphometrically. To confirm Vitamin D signaling activation, cultured lungs were processed for ISH and RT-qPCR and assessed for specific downstream targets. Results: In situ hybridization revealed that all members of the vitamin D signaling pathway are expressed throughout the early stages of chick lung branching. Furthermore, vitamin D induced the expression of cyp24a1, the main regulatory component of the pathway, thus validating the lung explant system. Lung explants treated with increasing doses of vitamin D displayed a statistically significant reduction in lung size and branching compared to controls. Conclusion: This study unveils, for the first time, the potential role of vitamin D signaling in the early stages of chick pulmonary branching. Overall, this study contributes to better understand the intricate molecular events that ultimately regulate branching morphogenesis. Parallel Oral Session - Neurosciences PS135 Astrocytes as Potential Targets to Reduce Neurotoxicity in Alzheimer's Disease Daniela Sofia Abreu1,2, Joana Isabel Gomes1,2, Hugo Vicente-Miranda3, Ana Maria Sebastião1,2, Maria José Diógenes1,2, Sandra Henriques Vaz1,2 1Instituto de Medicina Molecular João Lobo Antunes, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal, 2Instituto de Farmacologia e Neurociências, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal, 3Chronic Diseases Research Center, NOVA Medical School, Lisboa, Portugal Introduction: Astrocytes are implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), in which amyloid-ß (Aß) accumulation is observed [1]. Astrocytes respond to neuronal activity by releasing gliotransmitters through SNARE complex- dependent exocytosis [2], such as glutamate and D-serine, which bind to NMDA receptors (NMDARs), playing an important role in long-term potentiation (LTP) [1]. In AD, astrocytic glutamate activates extrasynaptic-NMDARs triggering pro-apoptotic signals, overcoming synaptic-NMDARs mediated survival signaling [3]. D-serine, synthesized from astrocytic L-serine, is a synaptic-NMDARs coagonist that lacks evidence of its primary source [4]. Therefore, we hypothesize that Aß accumulation dysreg- ulates astrocytes, exacerbating glutamate release and reducing D-ser- ine release, thereby modifying synaptic and extrasynaptic-NMDARs activation and thus suppressing the induction of LTP. Aim: Investigate whether astrocytic gliotransmitters release leads to aberrant engagement of LTP mechanism in AD. Methods: fEPSP were recorded in CA1 area of hippocampal slices from Wt and dn-SNARE (compromised SNARE-dependent gliotransmission [5]) mice after Aß1-42 oligomers(200 nM) [6], memantine(1 μM) (nonselective NMD AR antagonist that preferentially blocks extrasynaptic-NMDARs [7]), D-ser- ine(10 μM) [8] and L-serine(10/50 μM)[9] treatment. LTP was induced by theta-burst stimulation. Results: SNARE-dependent gliotransmission blockade abolished LTP deficits triggered by Aß exposure, similar to memantine, which also prevented Aß-induced LTP inhibition in Wt animals. Moreover, D-serine is released from astrocytes and controls NMDAR-dependent plasticity, as in dn-SNARE animals, LTP is not altered by D-serine precursor (L-serine) but increases 48.9% upon D-serine addition. In the presence of Aß, D-serine treatment restored LTP impairments in Wt animals and enhanced the neuroprotective potential of blocking gliotrans- mission in dn-SNARE animals. Conclusion: Our results suggest for the first time that: (i) the blockage of gliotransmission is protective in the Aß presence; (ii) astrocytes are the primary source of D-serine; (iii) D-serine increases LTP in slices pretreated with Aß, suggesting its promising neuroprotective effect for AD by regulating synap- tic-NMDARs. This work introduces new astrocytic mechanisms in AD that may contribute to the development of new therapeutic strategies. References 1. Armada-Moreira, A. et al. Front. Cell.
