Finally, the authors recapitulated the findings obtained in mice in human induced pluripotent cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) obtained from a patient with A2254V mutation in RyR2, which causes catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Following PDE2A and PDE4B overexpression in vitro, the authors observed dynamic changes in cAMP levels in caveolin-rich membrane microdomains and in RyR2, respectively. Remarkably, overexpression of PDE4B, but not PDE2A, reduces arrhythmia development in this hiPSC-CM model of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia induced by RyR2 Ca2+ leak. Overall, the results from Pavlaki et al. fill a gap in the knowledge regarding the molecular mechanisms involved in the protective effects exerted by specific PDE isoforms in HF and provide novel insights regarding our understanding of cAMP modification in specific microdomains in this disease. This evidence strongly suggests that interventions able to restore cAMP subcellular compartmentalization may represent a suitable therapeutic approach for HF treatment. However, there are still some remaining aspects that need to be clarified in future studies. The molecular mechanisms underlying the different localization of PDE2A3 and PDE4B3 in caveolin-rich and RyR2, respectively, should be elucidated. It will be important to study whether the protective effects of PDE isoform overexpression are mediated exclusively by cAMP distribution or also by other mechanisms. In addition to PKA, cAMP also activates other effectors such as Epac and protein kinase X-linked (PRKX)/protein kinase Y-linked (PRKY), exerting PKA-independent effects. It would be interesting to analyse how subcellular distribution of cAMP following PDE isoforms overexpression affects these substrates. PKA is also a known modulator of multiple substrates involved in cardiac hypertrophy, apoptosis, clearance of misfolded proteins.11 The different downstream targets of cAMP/PKA signalling that are modulated following PDE isoform overexpression should be analysed by a proteomic approach. Remarkably, a relevant open question is how PDE overexpression influences the subcellular distribution of 3′,5′-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels during HF. cGMP is an important intracellular messenger stimulated by natriuretic peptides (NPs) and nitric oxide (NO), which generally exerts opposite effects in cardiomyocytes as compared to cAMP signalling. It also represents a common target of drugs used for the treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Interestingly, PDE2 modulates both cAMP and cGMP, whereas PDE4 is specific for cAMP at physiological levels of expression. It will be important to check in the future whether differences in cGMP levels may also explain somehow the milder cardiac effects induced by PDE2A3 with respect to PDE4B3. The development of a drug able to maintain a balanced activity of cAMP and cGMP in their microdomains during cardiac remodelling remains a major challenge for the research field in the future. It will also be interesting to evaluate how PDE overexpression affects cAMP subcellular redistribution in other relevant experimental models of HFrEF, for example in mice undergoing chronic myocardial infarction. These results would extend the use of PDE modulators for the treatment of HFrEF with different aetiologies. Finally, data obtained in hiPSC-CMs are very impressive and open a new scenario for the development of precision medicine strategies for preventing life-threatening arrhythmias in subgroups of patients at high risk to develop HFrEF, such as those carrying genetic mutations in sarcomeric genes. Clinical studies with PDE3 inhibitors were reported to confer cardiac protective effects in the short-term, while detrimental in the long-term.12 The better understanding of the subcellular compartmentalization of specific PDE isoforms during the disease progression and their differential influences on cAMP levels will drive novel therapies focused on the modulation of a specific PDE isoform, rather than adopting a pan-PDE modulating strategy. title: Abstract 17263: Cardiac Myosin Binding Protein-C Phosphorylation Mitigates Pressure-Overload Heart Failure Despite Alterations in Calcium Handling
abstract: Heart failure with reduced ejection (HFrEF) fraction exhibits both systolic and diastolic dysfunctions; therefore, treatments that improve contractility and lusitropy will be helpful. Cardiac myosin binding protein-C (cMyBP-C), which is a thick filament protein, can increase rate of cross-bridge cycling by its phosphorylation status to enhance contractility and lusitropy. Consequently, we hypothesized that cMyBP-C phosphorylation mitigates HFrEF by preserving systolic and diastolic functions. We tested our idea by challenging WT cMyBP-C(tWT), phosphorylation-deficient cMyBP-C(t3SA):S273A/S282A/S302A, and phosphorylation-mimetic cMyBP-C(t3SD):S273D/S282D/S302D mouse models with trans-aortic constriction (TAC) to induce pressure-overload HFrEF. Survival at 5 weeks showed notable differences (tWT 75.6±6.7% n=41, t3SA 53.4±6.7% n=68, t3SD 92.1±4.4% n=38, p=0.00037). Serial echocardiography showed that cardiac structure and function deteriorated for all mouse models. In comparison to tWT at post-TAC week-5, t3SA demonstrated ventricular dilation and reduced ejection fraction (EF); conversely, t3SD exhibited better preservation of diastolic function (smaller E/Ea, where E=blood flow Doppler and Ea=tissue Doppler of peak myocardial relaxation velocity). Electrically paced intact papillary muscles from t3SA and t3SD demonstrated slower intracellular calcium decay (smaller decay rate constant kCa). Western blotting showed: (1) decreased calcium-ATPase (SERCA2a) expression in t3SA and t3SD, (2) lowest ryanodine receptor (RyR2) expression in t3SD, and (3) decreased calcium calmodulin kinase-2 phosphorylation (pCaMK2) only in t3SD. These calcium handling protein alterations likely prevented stronger rescue by cMyBP-C phosphorylation mimetic. Thus, cMyBP-C phosphorylation mimetic mitigated TAC-induced HFrEF (better survival and preservation of diastolic function) despite depression of calcium handling proteins.

title: Cardiac Myosin Activators: Up and Coming
abstract: This article refers to ‘Ribonucleotide reductase-mediated increase in dATP improves cardiac performance via myosin activation in a large animal model of heart failure’, by S. Kadota et al., published in this issue on pages XXX–XXX. Despite the central role of decreased contractile function in the pathogenesis of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), many promising inotropic agents have failed to demonstrate clinical benefits outside of cardiogenic shock.1 The dissociation between improved inotropy and clinical outcomes with these agents may be due to their mechanisms of action and effect on cellular energetics and calcium handling rather than a requisite adverse impact of increased myocardial contractility. Improved contractile function thus remains a viable therapeutic target. Myocardial contractility is produced at the cellular level by the interaction of myosin and actin filaments, with their relationship dynamics modulated by ATP, calcium, and regulatory proteins.2 The details of the myosin cycle are informative. Overall, the chemical energy of ATP hydrolysis is coupled to mechanical movement of ∼10 nm by each activated myosin head. In resting myocardium, troponin and tropomyosin bind to actin and prevent myosin attachment. Following myocyte depolarization, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum as well as imported from the extracellular space. The increased calcium binds troponin, allowing the myosin cycle to proceed. ATP binding releases myosin in its strongly bound post-contraction state from actin. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP resets the myosin lever arm to a cocked position. Release of the hydrolysed phosphate occurs concomitant with actin binding and is coupled to the force producing movement of the myosin lever arm. The cycle then ends with the dissociation of ADP from the myosin and the myosin–actin complex awaiting the arrival of the next ATP. Currently available inotropic agents including beta-adrenergic agonists, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and levosimendan, as well as many in the development pipeline including nitroxyl donors, modify this system either by increasing cellular calcium or by sensitizing the cardiomyocyte to endogenous calcium fluxes.1 Increased cytoplasmic calcium augments sarcomere activation and the velocity of contraction development (dP/dt). However, it also induces myocardial ischaemia and arrhythmias, clinically significant side effects of these agents. Some of the novel agents designed to improve cardiac contractility possess activities apart from their calcium-mediated myocardial effects, such as vasodilation, that may yet determine their utility. Enter the novel therapeutic class of cardiac myosin activators. These agents directly modulate the myosin and actin mechanism by accelerating the rate-limiting step of the myosin cycle, actin binding coupled to phosphate release. Although the force generated by each myosin head does not change, overall contractile function improves. Normally only a fraction of available myosin heads participate in each cardiac cycle; by speeding up the rate-limiting step, cardiac myosin activators allow a greater fraction of myosin to bind actin for each cycle, producing an augmented power stroke. The most advanced of the myosin activator class is omecamtiv mecarbil, a small molecule identified by optimization of compounds found by high-throughput screening of a biochemically reconstituted sarcomere.3 It increases the duration of cardiac contraction without increasing dP/dt, and functions independently of calcium homeostasis. Because it does not increase dP/dt, systole lengthens and diastole shortens. In canine models of both ischaemic and pacing-induced cardiac dysfunction, as well as a phase I healthy volunteer study and a phase II human HFrEF study, omecamtiv mecarbil produced concentration-dependent increases in stroke volume and LV ejection time.4-6 The dose-limiting effect is cardiac ischaemia at excessive concentrations, presumably due to diastolic shortening and consequent reductions in coronary perfusion. Initiation of a phase III programme awaits the final results of the Acute Treatment with Omecamtiv Mecarbil to Increase Contractility in Acute Heart Failure (ATOMIC-AHF) study, a completed phase II study of hospitalized patients with acute HFrEF (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01300013), and the Chronic Oral Study of Myosin Activation to Increase Contractility in Heart Failure (COSMIC-HF; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01786512), a phase II formulation and dose-finding study of oral omecamtiv mecarbil. In this setting, Kadota and colleagues have published here the use of a a distinct direct myosin activator in a large animal model.7 They tested an adeno-associated virus that delivers ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) gene therapy in an ischaemic porcine model of HFrEF. The foundation for this work was laid extensively by this same research group over the past two decades.8-10 The expressed RNR increases the intracellular fraction of 2-deoxy-ATP (dATP) which has been demonstrated to increase myosin activity in tissue culture and murine models. Cardiac-specific production of the enzyme complex is enabled with a troponin T promotor element, which ideally circumvents off-target effects, and it appears that <10% of the ATP pool needs to be replaced by dATP to facilitate these changes. Chronic RNR overexpression appears to lack adverse effects in a transgenic mouse model followed for 5 months.11 The dATP mechanism is similar to that of omecamtiv mecarbil in that both accelerate the rate-limiting step of myosin activation; however, some specific properties of dATP-mediated actuation are distinct. Biochemically, the change in substrate from ATP to dATP induces a conformational change in the actin-binding surface to allow increased myosin–actin attachment with stronger and quicker force generation. Inflated intracellular dATP levels increase myocardial contractile force and dP/dt without affecting lusitropy, thus preserving diastole. The study by Kadota and colleagues is the next step in the progression of this therapeutic. In a small unblinded pilot study of 17 Yucatan minipigs, ischaemic cardiomyopathy was generated by transient balloon occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery, a well-studied model system.7 However, this model is limited by a variable degree of systolic dysfunction (EF ranged from 30% to 55% following injury) and high mortality due to refractory arrhythmias (11 of the 28 pigs died prior to evaluation). Two weeks after the induction of HF, the surviving affected pigs were randomized to coronary infusion of adeno-associated virus (BB-R12 vector) or control solution. Echocardiographic and haemodynamic measurements were made until the pigs were euthanized 56 days following treatment. Although the variability of the model and the small number of animals used markedly limit the power of the study and its ability to recapitulate the findings of earlier work, there were modest but variable improvements in myocardial contractility and haemodynamics with high dose gene therapy, primarily apparent when analysing those animals that initially developed more severe systolic dysfunction. The authors should be applauded, as moving from bench to bedside is a colossal task. One major inflection point is the cumbersome transition to a large animal model to confirm advances characterized in cell culture or small animal settings. Although this study is small with significant weaknesses, the authors establish enough evidence to encourage expanded and more robust investigations.7 Nevertheless, hurdles and questions remain, and the enticing promise of this study needs to be balanced by the context of the findings. The intrinsic variability in this animal model and small sample sizes limit the robustness of these results, and the biological plausibility of the benefit could have been more adequately investigated. The effectiveness of the intervention on a biological level could have been reinforced by measuring RNR protein, addressing whether treatment actually increases dATP to the requisite levels in the myocardium, and demonstrating appropriate dose responsiveness. Furthermore, porcine–human differences may undermine the relevance of these results for predicting effects in humans. For instance, while dATP increases contractile force without calcium sensitization in porcine cultures, experiments with dATP in failing human heart tissue demonstrated a significant calcium sensitization effect.12, 13 In these experiments, the intracoronary injection was performed through the infarct-related artery; however, many patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy have chronic total coronary occlusions and may require delivery method alteration. Finally, the durability of this intervention will need to be characterized, as will the potential adverse and possibly neoplastic effects of the presence of supratherapeutic concentrations of dATP on the fidelity of DNA polymerase.14 Apart from the above concerns, the hope that greeted the conception of gene therapy as a therapeutic agent should be tempered with the reality of its implementation. Although multiple pre-clinical experiments have suggested the potential of adeno-associated virus gene therapy in cardiovascular disease, much of this territory is uncharted. Only one agent in the arena of cardiovascular disease has made it to phase II trials, gene therapy to boost the calcium level in the sarcoplasmic reticulum to increase contractility. However, the EF did not increase significantly with treatment in the Calcium Upregulation by Percutaneous Administration of Gene Therapy in Cardiac Disease (CUPID) phase II HFrEF trial, and recently the CUPID-2 phase II trial did not meet either its primary or its secondary endpoints.15 Additional obstacles universal to gene therapy trials have been identified. Because adeno-associated viruses are endemic, there is antiviral immunity in the human population that limits their clinical utility. In the Kadota trial, pigs with evidence of viral immunity were excluded, and though the proportion of pigs in which this was the case was not reported, in the human trial of cardiac gene therapy >50% of the population were excluded for this reason.15 Nonetheless, given the tremendous and growing size of the HF population, the authors should be praised for their achievement and urged to continue their investigations. One day this innovative therapeutic approach may improve outcomes for these extremely ill patients. title: Abstract 13856: Hydrogen Sulfide Donor, SG1002, Preserves Left Ventricular Global Function and Contractile Reserve in a Mouse Model of Doxorubicin Cardiotoxicity
abstract: Background: Despite being one of the most widely used chemotherapeutic agents, Doxorubicin [DOX] is limited by its dose-dependent side effects, including cardiotoxicity and heart failure (HF). Reactive oxygen species, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dysregulated autophagy have been proposed as potential mediators of cardiotoxicity. Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) has been shown to promote mitochondrial stability and reduce inflammation in the setting of myocardial infarction. Hypothesis: To determine if the orally active, slow-releasing H 2 S-compound SG1002 attenuates DOX-induced cardiotoxicity. Methods: Following baseline echocardiography, male C57BL mice (12 weeks old) were treated with DOX (5 doses of 5mg/kg, ip; once a week) over 5 weeks. One week before the first DOX treatment, mice were placed onSG1002-enriched chow to achieve a dosage of 40 mg/kg/day for the duration of the study. The control group received normal chow. Mice were followed up to 5 weeks after the last DOX treatment. Left ventricular (LV) function was assessed via echocardiography, including LV global longitudinal strain [GLS]. Contractile reserve was measured as a percent increase in LV ejection fraction (LVEF) following isoproterenol challenge (10ng/mouse). Results: The cumulative dose of 25mg/kg of DOX led to impaired cardiac contractile reserve in control mice, which was preserved in SG1002-fed mice (Fig.A). Despite no changes observed in LVEF throughout the study, LV GLS detected early signs of cardiac dyssynchrony following the DOX regimen (Fig.B). SG1002 treatment prevented the early decline in cardiac function following chemotherapy. Conclusion: Our results indicate that LV GLS and cardiac contractile reserve are able to detect early changes in LV contractility due to cardiotoxicity following DOX treatment, which can be prevented with SG1002. This further highlights the importance of early screening with advanced imaging to identify signs of cardiotoxicity.

title: Tenascin-C drives cardiovascular dysfunction in a mouse model of diabetic cardiomyopathy
abstract: Background: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a complex condition linked to diabetes, characterized by cardiac and vascular dysfunction, frequently concomitant with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The extracellular matrix glycoprotein Tenascin-C (TNC) has been found to be upregulated under diabetic conditions. However, the potential contributory role of TNC in the progression of DCM remains largely unclear. This study was designed to elucidate the role of TNC in the pathogenesis of DCM. Methods: Diabetes was induced in adult male wild-type (WT) and TNC knockout (TNC-KO) mice, through the administration of streptozotocin (50 mg/kg) for five consecutive days. At 18 weeks cardiac and aortic vascular function was evaluated using echocardiography and wire myography. Myocardium and plasma samples were collected for biochemical, histological, and molecular analyses. Cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts were used to investigate the impact of diabetes on TNC expression, inflammation, myocardial stiffness and function. Additionally, transcriptomic analysis of cardiac tissue by RNA-sequencing was conducted. Plasma TNC levels were assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay in cohorts of heart failure patients and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Results: TNC-KO diabetic mice showed preserved left ventricular systolic and diastolic function, significantly reduced cardiac fibrosis and mitigated endothelial dysfunction compared to WT diabetic animals. Compared with cardiomyocytes of diabetic WT animals, cardiomyocytes of TNC-KO mice developed less stiffness (Fpassive). Additionally, exposing mouse cardiomyocytes and human cardiac fibroblasts to high glucose stress (30 mM) led to a significant increase in TNC expression. Conversely, recombinant human TNC promoted pro-inflammatory and oxidative stress markers in cardiomyocytes. The role of TNC in fibrosis and DCM was found to involve pathways related to p53 signaling and Serpin1k, Ccn1, Cpt1a, and Slc27a1, as identified by RNA sequencing analysis. Additionally, plasma TNC levels were significantly elevated in patients with heart failure, irrespective of diabetes status, compared to healthy individuals. Conclusions: Our findings indicate that in diabetes, TNC contributes to cardiac contractile dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic disturbances in diabetic mouse heart. These results implicate the potential of TNC inhibition as a novel therapeutic approach for treating DCM.

title: Abstract P121: A Novel Delivery of Alpha-Calcitonin Gene Related Peptide (α-CGRP) Using Alginate Microcapsules Protects Against Pressure-Overload Induced Heart Failure
abstract: The cardioprotective role of α-calcitonin gene related peptide (α-CGRP), a 37-amino acid neuropeptide and potent vasodilator, in cardiac diseases has been established by our laboratory and others. Systemic delivery of α-CGRP decreases blood pressure in hypertensive humans, and improves hemodynamic variables in congestive heart failure (CHF) patients. However, the short half-life of the peptide (t 1/2 = ~5.5 min in serum) limits α-CGRP use in any long-term treatment regime. The present study utilized alginate-α-CGRP microcapsules for long-term continuous delivery of α-CGRP in a mouse CHF model. We used an electrospray method to prepare α-CGRP encapsulated alginate microcapsules approximately 200μm in size. The α-CGRP encapsulated microcapsules showed no cytotoxicity when incubated with the cardiac cell lines, HL-1 and H9c2 cells, for 7 days. Subcutaneous administration of microcapsules containing 150, 250, or 500μg α-CGRP lowered the systolic pressure up to 18 h, 3 days, and 7 days, respectively, in wild-type mice (measured by tail-cuff method), indicating that released α-CGRP remains biologically active. The cardioprotective effect of microcapsules released α-CGRP was examined using a transverse aortic constriction (TAC) induced pressure-overload mouse model of CHF. After two days of TAC, 500μl of alginate-α-CGRP microcapsules (containing 150μg α-CGRP) was administered in nine weeks old C57/BL6 mice on alternate days up to 28 days. Echocardiography data showed that microcapsule treatment of α-CGRP significantly preserved left ventricular fraction shortening (FS) and ejection fraction in the TAC mice (FS±SD: sham 47.2±1.5%, sham-alginate-α-CGRP 48.4±1.8%, TAC 29.5±1.4%, and TAC-alginate-α-CGRP 43.2±1.2%). α-CGRP delivery attenuated cardiac hypertrophy in TAC mice when reported as heart wt/tibia length (mg/mm±SD): sham 6.3±0.1, sham-alginate-α-CGRP 6.3±0.2, TAC 8.6±0.3, and TAC-alginate-α-CGRP 6.6±0.2. Alginate-only microcapsules did not affect these cardiac parameters. Our results show that α-CGRP delivery through alginate microcapsules protect hearts from cardiac failure. As alginate is immunologically inactive, the alginate microcapsules offer a new potential delivery paradigm for patients with heart failure.

title: The role of Follistatin-like 1 (Fstl1) in the developing heart
abstract: Congenital heart defects (CHD) are one of the most common type of birth defects affecting approximately 0.8% of live born infants. However, in as little as 15% of the cases of CHD an underlying genetic etiology has not been identified. Previous studies have suggested a role of Follistatin-like 1 (Fstl1) in congenital cardiac malformations and cardiovascular disease. Fstl1 is a secreted protein that is initially ubiquitously expressed during early heart development and then becomes gradually restricted to the non-myocardial component of the heart. In this thesis, we focus on trying to understand the function and the role of Fstl1 during heart development and disease. Genetic deletion of Fstl1 results in death of homozygous knock out mice at birth due to respiratory distress. These Fstl1 knock out mice show an array of abnormalities including cardiac, lung and skeletal defects. In the heart, loss of Fstl1 results in an increase in myocardial volume and prenatal transition from hyperplastic to hypertrophic growth. Based on a genome-wide phosphoproteome analysis, we uncovered a novel signaling pathway activated by Fstl1 involving RhoGTPase and the Gpr124 receptor. Ablation of Fstl1 from the endocardial/endothelial lineage revealed that Fstl1 is crucial in valve development and results in incompetent myxomatous mitral valves, which ensues in diastolic dysfunction, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and eventually death. Screening unresolved patients with CHD that resemble the mouse phenotype identified genetic variants but failed to identify mutations in the protein-coding region of Fstl1.

title: The absence of collagen VI reduces systolic function but paradoxically increases Ca 2+ release in the rat heart
abstract: Abstract Collagen VI has recently been strongly linked to poor outcomes in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction through increased endotrophin, a collagen VI-derived signalling molecule linked to fibrotic remodelling in cardiovascular disease. The mutation of collagen VI can result in Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy and Bethlem myopathy, pointing to critical function in muscle physiology. However, the role of collagen VI in the heart is poorly understood. In human heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, collagen VI is increased within the remodelled T-tubules, suggesting a possible role in tubular structure and Ca 2+ dynamics. To test this hypothesis, a global knockout of the collagen VI alpha 1 gene (Col6a1 -/- ) was generated in the rat. T-tubule structure and ryanodine receptor cluster organisation were unchanged, but echocardiography demonstrated reduced systolic function. Paradoxically, isolated cardiomyocytes from the Col6a1 -/- rat had increased Ca 2+ transient amplitude and increased sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ load. β-adrenergic stimulation further increased Ca 2+ transient amplitude and was associated with diastolic Ca 2+ release events in Col6a1 -/- cardiomyocytes. The disturbed Ca 2+ dynamics are remarkedly similar to defects found in cardiac myocytes of the MDX mouse that has non-functional dystrophin protein. Together, these data suggest that collagen VI contributes to regulation of Ca 2+ signalling in the heart through its linkage to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex.

title: Recent developments in cGMP research: From mechanisms to medicines and back
abstract: This article is part of a themed issue on cGMP Signalling in Cell Growth and Survival. To view the other articles in this section visit http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bph.v179.11/issuetoc Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) is a ubiquitous second messenger of wide-ranging physiological, pathophysiological, and pharmacological significance (Hofmann, 2020; Petraina et al., 2021; Sandner et al., 2021). Cellular receptors causing a rise in cGMP include two types of guanylyl cyclase, which convert GTP to cGMP and are activated by important cardiovascular and neuronal ligands. Transmembrane or “particulate” guanylyl cyclases (pGCs) are homodimers stimulated by extracellular peptides such as atrial, brain, or C-type natriuretic peptide (ANP, BNP, or CNP, respectively). Nitric oxide (NO)-sensitive guanylyl cyclases (NO-GCs) are heterodimeric cytosolic enzymes activated by binding of NO to their prosthetic haem group. The discovery of small-molecule modulators of NO-GC was a milestone in the field of cGMP pharmacology. NO-GC stimulators are allosteric regulators that enhance the activity of the reduced, haem-containing NO-GC. These compounds act independently of NO and synergistically with endogenous NO. NO-GC activators specifically bind to, and activate, the oxidized, haem-free form of NO-GC. cGMP targets downstream effectors such as cGMP-dependent protein kinases (cGKs, also known as PKGs) and cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels. cGMP-hydrolysing phosphodiesterases (PDEs) control the duration, amplitude, and spread of an intracellular cGMP signal. Some PDEs degrade both cGMP and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and some cAMP-PDEs are regulated by cGMP, providing a mechanism for cGMP-cAMP crosstalk. Pharmacological approaches targeting the NO/NO-GC and natriuretic peptide/pGC cascades have advanced to clinical management of various diseases such as erectile dysfunction (Goldstein et al., 1998), pulmonary arterial hypertension (Galie et al., 2005; Ghofrani et al., 2013), and more recently heart failure (HF) (Armstrong et al., 2020; McMurray et al., 2014). Indeed, out of 50 novel drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2021, two target the cGMP signalling system, that is, the NO-GC stimulator vericiguat to treat chronic HF with reduced ejection fraction and the pGC stimulator vosoritide to treat achondroplasia, a genetic disorder leading to short stature (visit Novel Drug Approvals for 2021 at https://www.fda.gov/drugs/). Both drugs are classified as first-in-class, having mechanisms of action different from those of existing medicines. Thus, the translational potential of preclinical findings with regard to new indications for cGMP-modulating drugs should be enormous. Although our knowledge about NO- and natriuretic peptide-dependent cGMP signal transduction and its diverse cellular effects has substantially increased in the last few decades, critical gaps remain. These gaps mostly concern the mechanisms and consequences of subcellular cGMP compartmentation as well as the identity and regulation of effectors, that mediate cGMP's effects in vivo (Cuello & Nikolaev, 2020). In addition to its short-term effects on, for example, smooth muscle contractility, cGMP also plays an important role in the homeostatic control of cell growth and survival. However, the positive and potentially also negative effects of acutely or chronically altered cGMP concentrations on tissue remodelling, degeneration and regeneration are not completely understood. Current research aims at identifying the relevant cell types and molecular mechanisms targeted by cGMP pathway modulation. To guide the future development of cGMP-based drugs, it appears important to consider the dynamics of endogenous cGMP profiles under the respective pathophysiological condition. This British Journal of Pharmacology themed issue on cGMP signalling in cell growth and survival assembles five review articles followed by eight original research papers from leading scientists that improve our understanding of the effects of endogenous and pharmacologically modulated cGMP signals on tissue repair and maintenance. We hope that the presented insights will lead to new strategies for the management of several age-related disorders including diseases of the heart, lungs, kidneys, nervous system, and hearing organ. The review section of the themed issue begins with a contribution by Friebe and Englert focusing on cGMP in the lung (Friebe & Englert, 2022). This organ expresses particularly high levels of NO-GC, but neither the cell types expressing NO-GC in the lung (e.g., pericytes, smooth muscle cells, and epithelial cells) nor the NO-GC-mediated mechanisms that affect lung physiology and pathophysiology are clear. The article discusses how pharmacological NO-GC activation in the lung may benefit patients suffering from obstructive airway diseases, acute respiratory distress syndromes, pulmonary hypertension, and pulmonary fibrosis. Interestingly, despite this obviously huge therapeutic potential, only a few drugs targeting cGMP in the lung have been successful so far, perhaps because NO-GC exists during disease progression in different isoforms and redox states, which are differentially targeted by NO-GC stimulators and activators. Lukowski et al. address the cytoprotective functions of the cGMP pathway in the heart, a topic that has attracted a lot of interest in recent years (Lukowski et al., 2022). They provide an up-to-date overview of the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms, highlighting that cGMP-mediated protection of cardiac muscle during ischaemia and reperfusion (I/R) injury in vivo requires activation of distinct K+ channels present in the inner compartment of the cardiomyocyte's mitochondria (Frankenreiter et al., 2017). Interestingly, cGMP signals are usually restricted to the cytosol and/or sub-sarcolemmal regions, which are distinct from the mitochondrial compartment of the cardiomyocyte. The article deals with the question of how signalling between cGMP-generating guanylyl cyclases and cGMP effectors in mitochondria can be established during cardiac I/R. The themed issue continues with two comprehensive review articles on cGMP-regulated neuronal and neurosensory functions. In the first contribution, Schmidt et al. discuss a CNP-cGMP-cGKI pathway that is critical for the correct branching of axons during embryonic development of the spinal cord, enabling neurons to connect with different targets in their vicinity (Schmidt et al., 2022). While genetic loss-of-function studies have clearly demonstrated the requirement of CNP, the CNP receptor GC-B, and cGKI for axon bifurcation, downstream mechanisms and targets phosphorylated by cGKI in these neurons remain poorly understood. The second part of the review summarizes how distinct cell populations in the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia contribute to cGMP-controlled processing of pain and itch during adulthood. It appears that in addition to the CNP-cGMP-cGKI pathway alternative cGMP signalling cascades also modulate nociception in the adult somatosensory system. The contribution by Marchetta et al. describes in detail what is known about the functions of the NO-GC- and pGC-stimulated pathways in the auditory system (Marchetta et al., 2022). They present evidence that basal hearing is largely unaffected by the cGMP cascade. Interestingly, however, ageing- and noise injury-induced dysfunctions, as well as the integrity of sound processing pathways in peripheral and central parts of the auditory system, are differentially affected by NO-GC- and pGC-induced cGMP formation. Overall, Marchetta et al. conclude that local delivery of NO-GC or pGC modulators to the inner ear may counteract hearing loss. However, such strategies need to consider that the manipulation of discrete cGMP pools may yield different and even opposite functional effects in different parts of the auditory system. A question that must be answered in future is if otoprotective functions of cGMP stem from neurons and/or the vasculature in close vicinity to the cochlea. The last review article discusses genetically encoded biosensors that can be used to monitor cGMP dynamics in living cells and organisms (Feil et al., 2022). Single-cell imaging of cGMP has revealed a pronounced heterogeneity of cGMP signalling both within a cell (also referred to as “compartmentation” or “microdomains”) as well as between different cells of a tissue or organ (also referred to as “cell-to-cell variability”). cGMP imaging has been instrumental for the recent discoveries of intercellular cGMP transfer and mechanosensitive cGMP generation, and it can be used to characterize the mode of action of cGMP-elevating drugs. The article summarizes the wide range of cGMP biosensors and their applications in cardiomyocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, and platelets, and discusses innovative future directions for optical mapping of cGMP in vitro and in vivo. The second part of this themed issue presents eight research papers that describe pharmacological cGMP modulation to preserve cellular functions in different physiological systems such as heart and kidney, new mechanisms of cGMP signalling, and novel optogenetic tools for manipulating cGMP locally in living cells by light. Previous work has concluded that PDE-5 and PDE-9 inhibition requires cGKI to oppose cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. In line with this model, cardiomyocyte-restricted deletion of cGKI provoked a more severe remodelling phenotype in mouse models of cardiac hypertrophy induced by angiotensin II or pressure overload. The beneficial effects attributed to cardiac cGKI are at odds with other studies suggesting that PDE-5 and cGKI in murine cardiomyocytes do not play major roles in pathological cardiac remodelling (Frantz et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2015; Lukowski et al., 2014; Patrucco et al., 2014). In this issue, Schwaerzer et al. (2022) add another piece to the puzzle of regulatory functions mediated by cGMP in the aged and diseased heart. In a cGKI mutant mouse model that expresses a constitutively active cGKI (cGKIR177Q/+ or Prkg1R177Q/+ mice), they find a mild acceleration of cardiac muscle fibrosis and more apoptotic myocytes in elderly (12-month-old) animals. In addition, left ventricular mass and other parameters of the cardiac structure were also affected by the presence of active cGKI in an age-related manner. Moreover, when young cGKIR177Q/+ animals were subjected to experimental models of cardiac hypertrophy, they developed more severe structural changes affecting cardiac chambers and walls, contractile dysfunction, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and cell death than control mice. Contrary to what has been known so far, the data of Schwaerzer et al. suggest that prolonged activation of cGKI may be harmful to aged or hemodynamically overloaded hearts. From a clinical perspective, caution is needed when considering long-term (over-)activation of cGKI for HF therapy. While the pathophysiological role of cGKI in myocardial hypertrophy is under debate, the preclinical study by Rüdebusch et al. (2022) substantiates the therapeutic potential of NO-GC stimulators such as riociguat in HF. Riociguat, clinically approved for patients with certain forms of pulmonary hypertension, acts as a NO sensitizer and also stimulates NO-GC in a NO-independent manner. In mice with established HF, riociguat (administered daily by oral gavage for 8 weeks) improved cardiac ejection fraction, decreased pathological myocardial fibrosis and myocyte cross-sectional area, and led to a reduction in heart weight as compared with non-treated mice. At the cellular level, riociguat opposed angiotensin II-induced pro-proliferative and pro-hypertrophic effects in cardiac fibroblasts and myocytes. Taken together, the results of Rüdebusch et al. support the concept that HF is associated with reduced bioavailability of NO and, therefore, pharmacological stimulation of NO-GC may prove beneficial under this condition. cGMP signals are usually terminated by the activity of cGMP-hydrolysing PDEs. In addition to this mechanism, Grange et al. (2022) followed up on the idea that cGMP efflux might also contribute to the kinetics of a cGMP-driven response. To test whether efflux of cGMP involves multidrug resistance-associated proteins (MRPs), the authors applied MK571, an inhibitor of MRP4 and MRP5, to human coronary artery smooth muscle cells, murine aorta, and a mouse model of pressure overload-induced HF. The key findings of this study are as follows: (i) cGMP generated via the ANP-pGC pathway in coronary artery smooth muscle cells is subject to significant MK571-sensitive cGMP efflux; (ii) vasorelaxant responses to ANP are amplified by MK571; (iii) although MK571 alone did not alter blood pressure, hypotensive responses to ANP were significantly enhanced by this compound; and (iv) MK571 reversed multiple parameters of cardiac dysfunction in mice with pressure overload-induced HF. These beneficial effects of MK571 were associated with a reduced plasma cGMP concentration, which indicates a relevant contribution of cGMP efflux via MRPs to pathological changes in the intracellular and extracellular cGMP equilibrium. It will be exciting to see if pharmacological MRP inhibition can be established to enhance or optimize the benefits of cGMP-based therapies. Compared with NO-GC stimulators, the clinical development of NO-GC activators is less advanced. NO-GC activators bind to the haem-free NO-unresponsive NO-GC, which might be increasingly formed under conditions of pathological oxidative stress. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with decreased NO bioavailability and increased oxidative stress, and NO-GC gain of function has been linked to a higher glomerular filtration rate and lower risk for CKD (Emdin et al., 2018). As such, CKD is an interesting indication, particularly for NO-GC activators. NO-GC stimulators and activators have been tested in several preclinical models of kidney diseases and resulted in reduced proteinuria and/or albuminuria and decreased renal glomerulosclerosis and fibrosis. In this issue, Harloff et al. (2022) explore the first-generation NO-GC activator cinaciguat in a mouse model of diabetic nephropathy, the leading cause of end-stage renal disease worldwide. Cinaciguat inhibited the progression of renal damage by attenuating glomerular and fibrotic changes, particularly in diabetic mice lacking endothelial NO synthase. In primary mesangial cells exposed to diabetic conditions, cinaciguat increased the level of NO-GC, presumably by binding to its haem pocket and thereby leading to the stabilization of the protein. Furthermore, cinaciguat suppressed the expression of thrombospondin 1, a key activator of transforming growth factor β and profibrotic processes in the diseased kidney. The clinical value of cinaciguat has recently been challenged in patients with acute HF (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01064037). Thus, cinaciguat appears to be useful to elucidate molecular mechanisms in preclinical models, but it may be not suitable to treat patients. New NO-GC activators are currently in development which show improved pharmacokinetics and a lower potential to cause hypotension (Sandner et al., 2021). Runcaciguat is a novel potent and selective second-generation NO-GC activator, which has great potential to prevent the decline of kidney function (Benardeau et al., 2021). In this issue, Stehle et al. (2022) studied the kidney-specific mechanisms behind the renoprotective effects of runcaciguat. They measured cGMP levels in real time in kidney slices of transgenic cGMP sensor mice and show that the runcagiguat-like compound BAY-453 indeed increases the glomerular cGMP concentration in the presence of oxidative stress. Moreover, runcaciguat induced dilation of glomerular arterioles and improved renal blood flow under disease-relevant oxidative stress conditions. Thus, runcaciguat's mode of action appears to be the dilation of renal blood vessels, presumably by activation of NO-GC in vascular smooth muscle cells. This may increase renal blood flow, thereby, slowing down the progression of kidney disease. NO-GC activators could represent a new therapeutic approach for the treatment of CKD patients. title: The heart during iron deficiency: a non‐rechargeable battery?
abstract: This article refers to ‘Cardiac energetics in patients with chronic heart failure and iron deficiency: an in-vivo 31P magnetic resonance spectroscopy study’ by F. Papalia et al., published in this issue on pages 716–723. Systemic iron deficiency (ID) is detected in approximately 50% of patients with chronic heart failure. Regardless of the presence of anaemia, ID is associated with impaired exercise capacity, reduced quality of life and a worse prognosis. Treatment with intravenous iron results in improved symptoms and reduced rehospitalizations, also independent of haemoglobin levels. This is likely because of the essential role of iron beyond the carriage of oxygen as part of haemoglobin. Iron is essential for cellular oxygen storage and metabolism, redox cycling, and as an enzymatic cofactor in a wide range of cellular processes. Metabolic processes including the citric acid cycle, β-oxidation pathway and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation are reliant on iron containing enzymes. These metabolic processes are the resource of >90% of the hearts adenosine triphosphate (ATP), a total of 1 mM ATP per second. In case of a metabolic arrest, the entire cardiac energy reserve would be exhausted within seconds. High energy demanding tissues such as the heart, are therefore theoretically vulnerable to the effects of ID. This has been exemplified in several studies. On a cellular level, iron-deficient human cardiomyocytes have an impaired mitochondrial respiration, lower ATP levels and impaired contraction and relaxation.1 In vivo mouse studies of cardiac specific ID showed mitochondrial dysfunction resulting in cardiac failure and increased mortality rates.2, 3 All of the mentioned effects could be ameliorated by the administration of iron. The only study investigating actual patient heart tissue, using ex-vivo tissue homogenate analyses, showed a reduced activity of several enzymes essential for the citric acid cycle and protection against reactive oxygen species.4 Remarkably, respiratory chain enzyme activity was preserved in that study. Until now, in vivo assessment of cardiac mitochondrial function in human patients with heart failure and ID was lacking. In vivo myocardial energy metabolism can be assessed using phosphorus-31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P-MRS), a non-invasive imaging technique. Metabolites containing phosphorus, such as ATP and phosphocreatine (PCr) can be quantified in real time. While the absolute quantification of these metabolites requires an ex-vivo concentration reference, the PCr/ATP ratio has been proven a relevant measure of cardiac metabolism. PCr fulfills the function of an intracellular battery, providing the cardiomyocyte with an energy buffer in case of increasing ATP demand5 (Figure 1). In times of relative rest, the PCr buffer will be replenished by predominantly oxidative phosphorylation and excess ATP. A lower PCr/ATP ratio has been associated with metabolic stress conditions such as heart failure, cardiac ischaemia, obesity and diabetes.5 In this issue of the Journal, Papalia et al.6 provide the first data on myocardial energy metabolism in patients with heart failure and ID. Patients from four centres with stable New York Heart Association (NYHA) class I to III heart failure based on non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, with no drug or dose changes for 4 weeks and a left ventricular ejection fraction <45% were included. Healthy volunteers consisted of age and gender-matched subjects without known medical or drug history. A total of 50 subjects were prospectively studied, resulting in reliable 31P-MRS spectra in 45 subjects: 12 patients with heart failure with normal iron levels, 22 patients with heart failure and ID, and 11 healthy volunteers. ID was defined as a ferritin <100 µg/L or 100–300 µg/L with a transferrin saturation <20%, consistent with the definition used in the largest clinical trials. The 31P-MRS spectra were obtained from the interventricular septum. The PCr/ATP ratio of patients with ID was significantly lower compared to patients with heart failure and normal iron levels or healthy volunteers (Figure 1). Patients with ID had significantly higher NYHA class and were more often in atrial fibrillation, though univariable adjustment for these variables, as well as haemoglobin and others, did not alter the observed differences. In the patients with heart failure, the PCr/ATP ratio correlated with ferritin levels and inversely with NYHA class. Though not the primary endpoint, no differences were observed between patients with or without anaemia, or between healthy volunteers and heart failure patients without ID. The study provides the first human in vivo confirmation that cardiac energetics might be, at least partly, responsible for the signs and symptoms observed in patients with ID. Previous data on the association of iron status with cellular energetics are derived from animal studies or human studies utilizing skeletal muscle. Haddad et al.3 studied a mice model of mild cardiomyocyte specific ID. At baseline, these mice have normal PCr/ATP ratios and show no obvious clinical phenotype. Cardiac stress reveals a phenotype: myocardial infarction results in more severe heart failure compared to wild-type animals and a dobutamine stress test results in a lower PCr/ATP ratio, an impaired mitochondrial respiration rate, and a lack of inotropic reserve.3 In humans, the cardiac PCr/ATP ratio correlates well with disease severity.5 Patients with aortic valve disease or ischaemia without symptoms of heart failure have normal PCr/ATP ratios, while patients who do present with heart failure signs and symptoms have a reduced PCr/ATP ratio, which also correlates with NYHA class.7, 8 Exercise intolerance also correlates with skeletal muscle energetic abnormalities.9 At low exercise intensity, patients with heart failure show impaired oxidative metabolism, with the fastest PCr decline rate during exercise in patients with a preserved left ventricular ejection fraction.9 The PCr recovery phase is also markedly prolonged in these patients.9 In another study, ID was associated with even worse skeletal muscle bioenergetics, exemplified by an increased PCr loss and acidification during exercise.10 The administration of two doses of 500 mg of intravenous iron in 13 patients with heart failure and ID resulted in improved maximal isometric force, but not in metabolic alterations.10 The FERRIC-HF II randomized controlled trial studied the effects of iron isomaltoside on the skeletal muscle PCr recovery rate after exercise in 40 patients with heart failure and ID.11 In only 2 weeks, the PCr recovery rate improved significantly in patients receiving iron compared to placebo, as did their NYHA class and symptoms of dyspnoea.11 The changes in PCr recovery rate correlated with improvements in ferritin level, 6-min walking test distance and peak oxygen consumption, but not haemoglobin, and was independent of baseline haemoglobin levels.11 The current study by Papalia et al. illustrates that iron status is associated with poor cardiac energetics in patients with heart failure. It provides evidence for local, myocardial consequences of ID, potentially explaining the signs and symptoms observed in these patients. The study also highlights the existing knowledge gaps. Iron status is assessed using circulating biomarkers (ferritin and transferrin saturation) which have either been used in large clinical trials12 or validated against bone marrow.13 However, correlation of these circulating biomarkers with cardiac iron status might be absent.14, 15 A measure of cardiac iron status, such as T2* quantification, is therefore highly desirable for future studies. Confounding by disease severity or NYHA class might explain the reported association, although statistical adjustment argued against it. Relatively little is known about ID in patients with heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction, while they might be the most severely impacted. Finally, the effects of intravenous iron administration on the heart, and specifically on cardiac energy metabolism are unknown. To improve our understanding of disease mechanisms and the beneficial effects of treatment, future studies should assess cardiac iron status and response to treatment in patients with heart failure. Both patients with a reduced and a preserved ejection fraction should be included. Exercise or pharmacological stress might be required to truly understand the associations of symptoms to pathological disease mechanisms. For now, although we do not fully understand all mechanisms in play yet, we should continue to treat our patients with heart failure and ID using intravenous iron to improve symptoms and reduce rehospitalizations.12 Conflict of interest: N.G.B. received speaker fees from Vifor Pharma.

title: A novel approach to modelling acute cardiac decompensation in rats
abstract: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) of pre-existing heart failure (HF) is predictive of adverse outcomes. In patients older than 65, ADHF is the leading cause of hospitalization with a high in-hospital mortality of up to 10%.1 Repeated episodes of ADHF shorten the residual life expectancy even more.2 Notably, despite clinical recompensation, ADHF causes structural and functional cardiac damage.3 However, there is still a lack of established treatment options and therapy algorithms for ADHF patients. ADHF can be triggered by multiple factors like myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmias, or arterial hypertension.4 However, few rodent models reflect this scenario.5 In most models, HF develops gradually due to a single stimulus. Here, we propose a novel rat model of HF that combines two established protocols to achieve both the development of chronic HF and the induction of ADHF. As a first hit, we induced HF using an aortocaval fistula (ACF).6 As a second hit, we added a hypertensive stimulus using deoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA) and salt loading to temporarily impair cardiac function.5 Once this hypertensive stimulus had ceased, a recompensation phase followed (Figure 1A). A novel HF model that permits the induction of decompensation and investigation of subsequent partial recompensation in rats. (A) Clinical background and study protocol. Two-hit rat model with volume overload and hypertensive stress caused by an infra-renal ACF and subsequent DOCA with salt loading. Numbers 0–3 indicate the respective time of analysis, in brackets the number of rats per group. (B) Longitudinal assessment of echocardiographic diastolic LV posterior wall thickness (LVPW), LVEF, and E/e′, as well as plasma BNP and albuminuria (top to bottom). (C) Endpoint characteristics showing body weight, normalized heart, liver, and lung weight, as well as histological analysis of cardiac fibrosis (Sirius red). (D) Cardiac gene expression of natriuretic peptide B (Nppb), natriuretic peptide A (Nppa), collagen type I alpha 1 chain (Col1a1), fibronectin 1 (Fn1), and cellular communication network factor 2 (Ccn2). (E) Principal component analysis of plasma proteomes across time points 0–3. (F) Heatmap shows z-scored mean protein abundances at time points 1, 2, and 3 for significantly altered proteins in ACF + DOCA by generalized additive modelling. Comparisons in (B) by repeated measurement two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc test, P-values from Sham vs. ACF-DOCA in red, Sham vs. ACF in blue, and ACF vs. ACF-DOCA in purple, only P < 0.05 is shown. (C and D) P-values from one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc test. Each symbol represents one animal, n = 6 for Sham, n = 7 for ACF, and n = 12 for DOCA + ACF in all plots. The present data suggest that the combination of an ACF with temporary DOCA/salt in rats creates a decompensation scenario that recapitulates typical features of human ADHF, such as gradual loss of cardiac function, and may thus be valuable for future pre-clinical testing. Experiments were performed in accordance with the German/European law for animal protection (Directive 2010/63/EU) and approved by the local ethics committee (G0195/14). Rats were maintained on a 12:12 h day:night cycle with constant access to food and water. HF was induced in 10-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rats by a medium-sized infra-renal ACF,6 established by puncturing the aorta with an 18G hypodermic needle and advancing it into the vena cava, followed by sealing the puncture with cyanoacrylate glue. Persistence of ACF was confirmed by Doppler sonography. After 3 weeks, rats received a second stimulus with subcutaneous 21-day release 100 mg DOCA pellets and 1% NaCl in drinking water. Cessation of DOCA release and NaCl supplementation allowed the investigation of a 2-week recompensation phase. Operations and echocardiography were performed in isoflurane anaesthesia (2.0–2.4% isoflurane–air mixture). For the operations, analgesia was administered pre-emptively with carprofen [5 mg/kg subcutaneous (s.c.)] and after the operation with metamizole for 3 days in drinking water (1.33 mg/mL). Sham- and ACF-operated rats without DOCA/salt served as controls (Figure 1A). For organ collection, rats were anaesthetized using isoflurane (2.0–2.4%) and carprofen (5 mg/kg s.c.) and subsequently decapitated. Longitudinal examinations (plasma, echocardiography) were performed at baseline, before/after DOCA/salt, and after recompensation (endpoint). Plasma was analysed using the rat BNP 45 ELISA Kit (Abcam, Cambridge, UK) and the mouse OLINK proteomics exploratory panel (95% cross-reactivity according to the manufacturer). Histology and gene expression were analysed according to published protocols.7 Longitudinal data were analysed by repeated measurement two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni post hoc test and endpoint data by one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc test. Adjusted P-values <0.05 were considered significant. For proteomics, analytes with >30/99 samples below the limit of detection were filtered. Generalized additive models were used for univariate analysis. P-values were false discovery rate adjusted according to Benjamini–Hochberg. HF development was monitored by echocardiography. After ACF, left ventricular (LV) wall thickness increased with a preserved LVEF (Figure 1B). ADHF induction by DOCA/salt further increased LV wall thickness and significantly reduced LV ejection fraction (LVEF). While the recuperation of LVEF after ADHF indicated a partial recovery, LV wall thickness as a structural measure remained at a high level, with the highest values in ACF + DOCA. Interestingly, an increase in E/e′ ratio as a surrogate of LV end-diastolic pressure was only seen in ACF + DOCA after ADHF and remained at an elevated level after the recompensation phase (Figure 1B). Plasma natriuretic peptide B (BNP) showed a similar pattern (Figure 1B). ADHF induced by DOCA/salt resulted in long-term structural changes of the heart. Increased lung and liver weight indicated organ congestion (Figure 1C). Histological analysis revealed aggravated fibrosis (Figure 1C), confirmed by the elevated expression of markers of fibrosis and hypertrophy (Figure 1D). In addition, ADHF triggered albuminuria with only moderate recovery (Figure 1B). Using targeted plasma proteomics from longitudinal samples, we observed a phase-specific clustering of plasma proteomes in ACF + DOCA compared with Sham and ACF, with the greatest deviation from baseline after ADHF and subsequent partial recovery (Figure 1E). Univariate analysis revealed 33 of 62 detected proteins (53%) with a dysregulated pattern over time in ACF + DOCA, 15 proteins (24%) commonly dysregulated in ACF and ACF + DOCA, and only 4 proteins (6%) in ACF alone (Figure 1F). Interestingly, plasma proteome changes partially mirrored those previously described in human cohorts.8–10 Among others, we observed changes in TNFRSF11B (osteoprotegerin), which was recently shown to predict cardiovascular events in stable cardiovascular disease.10 Similarly, vascular endothelial growth factor D, implicated in cardiovascular outcomes,8 and transforming growth factor beta 1, a known marker for cardiac fibrosis,9 were among the 33 altered proteins. The full dataset can be obtained from Zenodo for further comparison or validation. We present a novel HF rat model that enables the precise induction of ADHF with subsequent recompensation. Despite a partial recovery of cardiac function, an aggravated structural cardiac remodelling in rats that have undergone ADHF was observed. Decompensation and partial recovery were likewise mirrored in the plasma proteome. Limitations complicate the interpretation of cardiac gene expression. First, the combination of DOCA and salt is known to have direct effects on the heart. Secondly, gene expression was measured after recompensation rather than at the time of acute decompensation. Of note, we observed a low mortality (number of pre-specified humane endpoints reached: n = 3 after ACF surgery and n = 1 in the decompensation phase). We therefore believe the model is suited for various contexts. Taken together, our model reflects the clinical features of HF with episodes of ADHF. The sequential order of the two stimuli may allow further stage-specific investigations of HF pathophysiology. In addition, this model may be suitable for studying novel drug candidates for the prevention or treatment of ADHF. The data underlying this article will be shared on request to the corresponding author. The proteomics data and analysis underlying this article are available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10809160.

title: Abstract 17570: Therapeutic Impact of Autophagy-inducing Peptide on Pressure Overload-induced Heart Failure
abstract: Tat-Beclin1 (TB1), which binds human immunodeficiency virus-1 Nef, is a potent inducer of autophagy. We investigated the therapeutic potential of TB1 in the heart during pressure overload (PO). At baseline, treatment of cardiomyocytes (CMs) with 25 μM TB1 significantly increased both GFP/RFP double positive (Yellow) LC3 puncta (8.3±1.1 vs 1.4±0.2, P<0.05) and RFP LC3 puncta (4.2±1.1 vs 1.5±0.3, p<0.05) compared to treatment with Tat-scrambled (TS). After treatment for 2 weeks with TB1 or TS at 20 mg/kg daily, GFP-LC3 puncta were significantly increased in mouse hearts with TB1 compared to those with TS, with (31.6±5.0 and 20.3±5.9, p<0.05) or without chloroquine (21.7±4.3 and 8.1±2.2, p<0.05), indicating that TB1 stimulates autophagy in the heart. We investigated whether lysosomal clearance of mitochondria, reflecting mitochondrial autophagy, is stimulated by TB1, using Mito-Keima. Puncta with a high ratio of excitation at 560/440 nm co-localized with Alexa 488 Dextran, reflecting lysosomal localization of Mito-Keima, were significantly increased after TB1 compared to after TS treatment (5.68±1.18 vs 1.37±0.76, p<0.05). In order to evaluate the effect of TB1 upon the heart during PO, C57BL/6J mice were subjected to i.p. injections of TB1 or TS for 2 weeks, and the mice were sacrificed after 1 week. Ejection fraction (EF) was maintained (78.3±1.2 vs 63.3±3.0, p<0.05), lung weight/tibial length was lower (7.9±0.3 vs 8.2±0.2, p<0.05), the pressure gradient was greater (89.3±4.4 vs 71.8±4.3, p<0.05), and the end diastolic pressure (EDP) was lower (8.2±0.9 vs 11.5±1.5, p<0.05) in TB1- than in TS-treated mice. Mitochondrial ATP production was better preserved in TB1- than in TS-treated mice (1.72±0.16 vs 1.00±0.16, p<0.05). Mitochondrial DNA content (0.54±0.05 vs 1.00±0.11, p<0.05) and the Cox1 level in mitochondria (0.47±0.11 vs 1.00±0.18, p<0.05) were lower in TB1- than in TS-treated mice, consistent with increased degradation of mitochondria. In EM analyses of the mouse heart, autophagosomes containing mitochondria were observed after TB1 treatment, but not TS treatment. These results suggest that TB1 induces general autophagy and mitophagy in the heart and acts protectively against cardiac dysfunction after PO.

title: Abstract Wed035: Foxe1 Loss of Function Contributes to Adverse Remodeling in the Heart
abstract: Cardiac fibrosis is a major determinant in diastolic dysfunction, signified by excessive extracellular matrix deposition. This can lead to heart failure, especially heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Currently, there are no specific treatments targeting HFpEF or its underlying cardiac fibrosis, warranting the urgent need for identifying new and novel therapeutic approaches. Forkhead box protein 1 (Foxe1) is a transcription factor, crucial for cell proliferation and differentiation in thyroid development. Recently we determined that Foxe1 functional loss in the thyroid induced significant fibrosis and increased mast cell number. Interestingly Foxe1 is also abundantly expressed in the heart, yet the effect of Foxe1 functional loss in the heart has never been investigated. We aimed to determine the effect of Foxe1 loss on cardiac structure and function. We hypothesized that the loss of Foxe1 induces cardiac fibrosis by encouraging the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes and inflammatory response. Hearts from 20 week old-tamoxifen induced Foxe1 deficient mice were analyzed for fibrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration. Age matched wild type mice were included as control. Additionally, isolated mouse cardiac fibroblasts were treated with transforming growth factor b1 (TGF-b1, 30ng/mL) as a pro-fibrotic stimulus, and Foxe1 gene level measured. Also, mouse cardiac fibroblasts were cultured for chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing (ChIP-Seq) analysis against Foxe1. Our results showed that collagen volume fraction was increased in Foxe1 deficient mice compared to WT, indicative of cardiac fibrosis (1.2±0.35 vs 0.94±0.15%, p=0.038, n=10). Foxe1 deficient mice also had increased mast cell numbers (23.2±3.35 vs 11.6±3.91, p=0.001, n=5) and pro-inflammatory Mac2 + CD86 + macrophages (18.2±4.2 vs 7.6±1.12, p=0.04, n=5) and decreased anti-inflammatory CD206 + macrophages (12.4±1.32 vs 103.4±5.99, p<0.0001, n=5) compared to WT. TGF-b1 treatment in mouse cardiac fibroblasts decreased Foxe1 gene level as early as 2 hours (0.66±0.03 vs 1.12±0.05, p=0.01, n=6), indicative of direct and rapid effects of TGF-b1 on Foxe1 gene. ChIP-seq analysis on cardiac fibroblasts revealed that Foxe1 binds to gene related to fibrosis and cell motility such as nhlrc2 , clasp2 and mycn. In conclusion, cardiac Foxe1 functional loss induces fibrosis and inflammation in the heart, possibly due to Foxe1 inability to prevent the transcription of some fibrotic genes.

title: APOL1 Nephropathy Risk Variants Through the Life Course: A Review
abstract: Two variant alleles of the gene apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1), known as risk variants (RVs), are a major contributor to kidney disease burden in those of African descent. The APOL1 protein contributes to innate immunity and may protect against Trypanosoma, HIV, Salmonella, and leishmaniasis. However, the effects of carrying 1 or more RVs contribute to a variety of disease processes starting as early as in utero and can be exacerbated by other factors (or "second hits"). Indeed, these genetic variations interact with environmental exposures, infections, and systemic disease to modify health outcomes across the life span. This review focuses on APOL1-associated diseases through the life-course perspective and discusses how early exposure to second hits can impact long-term outcomes. APOL1-related kidney disease typically presents in adolescents to young adults, and individuals harboring RVs are more likely to progress to kidney failure than are those with kidney disease who lack APOL-1 RVs. Ongoing research is aimed at elucidating the association of APOL1 RV effects with adverse donor and recipient kidney transplant outcomes. Unfortunately, there is currently no established treatment for APOL1-associated nephropathy. Long-term research is needed to evaluate the risk and protective factors associated with APOL1 RVs at different stages of life.
