title: Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy: a fertile field for research
abstract: During the 1960s, our research group at the National Heart Institute (now the NHLBI) focused on two seemingly different areas—the pathophysiology in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and the basic mechanisms of heart failure in animal models with a focus on mitochondria. It certainly did not occur to us that these two areas were closely related. The former was summarized in a previous article,1 while the latter is discussed here. Cells with nuclei (eucaryotic cells) are believed to have appeared on earth about 2.5 billion years ago, and for many years were anaerobic, with little energy for cellular development or specialized functions essential for plants and animals. This situation changed radically about 1.5 billion years ago, when these cells engulfed procaryotic cells, which probably were primitive bacteria. The two cell types fused, with the larger eucaryotic cells serving as the ‘host’ cells and the procaryotic cells the ‘guest’ cells. The latter were discovered near the end of the 19th century and were named mitochondria (M). In this arrangement, the host cells provide physical protection for the M which are the ‘power plants’ for the hosts. This partnership of ‘cells within cells’ has been so successful that it led to the presence of M in virtually all cells in both plants and animals. M are unique organelles that are the size of most bacteria and reside in the host cells’ cytoplasm. Their structure was first elucidated by electron microscopy in 1945. M differ from other intracellular structures because they are enclosed within two membranes like the host cells. Importantly, they have separate genomes that are arranged in a circular manner. M possess 37 genes and are transmitted only maternally; their DNA is referred to as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). They are greatly outnumbered by the host cells’ genes whose DNA is referred to as nuclear DNA (nDNA) that are transmitted by both parents. More than 1300 nDNAs affecting M have been discovered. The number of M per host cell varies, depending on the latter’s energy requirements. The heart, brain and skeletal muscles have the greatest energy requirements, and the cells of these organs have the highest concentrations of M in their cytoplasm; each cell may contain hundreds or even more M. M are present, albeit in lower numbers, in other cells as well. While mutations occur in both genomes, they are far more frequent in the mtDNA. The principal function of M is to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) by combining adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate, i.e. oxidative phosphorylation, through a series of reactions referred to as the electron transport chain. This critically important process can be blocked by specific variants of nDNA as well as mtDNA, which can cause or contribute to the development of M dysfunction, which in turn may kill or interfere with the function of the host cell. The resultant M disease (MD), which was previously referred to as respiratory chain disease,2 may affect many organs. In addition to oxidative phosphorylation M have other cellular functions, including preservation of cellular Ca++ concentrations which control sarcomeric contraction and relaxation. M also play important roles in the regulation of cellular apoptosis and of innate immunity. Given these multiple functions of M it is apparent that MD can affect most body systems. The first patient with MD was described by Luft et al.3 in 1962. MD affecting the heart is generally referred to as mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (MCM). Meyers et al.4 have provided a useful working definition of this condition: ‘Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy can be described as a myocardial condition characterized by abnormal heart-muscle structure, function, or both, secondary to genetic defects involving the mitochondrial respiratory chain, in the absence of concomitant coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease, or congenital heart disease.’ MCM most frequently causes non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Usually, late in the course of the condition, ventricular dilatation with reduced ejection fraction, leading to dilated cardiomyopathy, may occur. MCM may also be responsible for ventricular non-compaction, a variety of arrhythmias, disturbances in conduction and sudden cardiac death. While MD may be isolated to the heart, more often it causes dysfunction of other organs as well, including a variety of central nervous system disorders, metabolic abnormalities, and endocrinopathies, and frequently is accompanied by elevated blood concentrations of lactic acid and pyruvate. Cardiac involvement is also present in a number of specific MD syndromes such as the Bath, Leigh, and Kearns–Sayre syndromes. Prominent among these syndromes is myopathy encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes known as the MELAS syndrome.2 MD can affect one or more organ systems, and several clinical manifestations in each have been described.5 Since it is usually a genetic disorder, it is important to obtain a family history. MCM ranges widely in severity, from an asymptomatic condition to death in a multi-organ crisis. The diagnosis of MD may be confirmed by biopsy, generally of skeletal muscle, its examination by electron microscopy combined with identification of typical genetic abnormalities, and by immunohistopathological analysis.6 MD is considered an infrequent condition with an incidence of 1 in about 5000 persons. Since approximately one-third of the affected have MCM, the latter might occur in only 1 in 15 000. However, based on my personal observation, the diagnosis is frequently not considered because patients with this condition present with a variety of puzzling manifestations. Centres or individual physicians with a special interest in the condition have shown that M disease is much more common than previously thought. For example, Savvatis et al.7 reported a multi-institutional registry of 600 adults with genetically confirmed MD. Of these, 230 (38.3%) had cardiac involvement. At a median follow-up of 6.7 years, all-cause mortality occurred in 15.8% of the total group, and 20% of the 230 with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy experienced a major adverse cardiac event. MCM is more common in children and adolescents than in adults. Imai-Okazaki et al.8 reported 223 patients <18 years with a confirmed genetic diagnosis of MD. Of these, 46 (21%) had MCM. The entire group was followed for a median of 36 months and the subgroup with MCM exhibited a higher mortality rate than did the patients without cardiac involvement. By multivariate analysis of the patients with MD, left ventricular hypertrophy, neonatal onset, and chromosomal aberrations were independent risk factors for MCM. Patients in whom MD is present or likely to be so should be referred to a centre or physician(s) with experience with MCM. First- and second- degree relatives of patients likely to have this condition should be screened for MCM. No specific therapy for MCM is currently available. However, published practice guidelines should be followed. For example, when present, diabetes, hypertension, or heart failure should be treated vigorously. Supportive care and good nutrition are indicated. Patients with intractable heart failure may be considered for insertion of a ventricular assist device or cardiac transplantation.2,5 M transplantation refers to the transfer of normal, isolated M which can be autologous or allogenic. Such transplantation can reduce cardiomyocyte death following ischaemia-reperfusion injury in animal experiments but have not been reported in humans at the time of this writing.9 Research on M function and dysfunction has been hindered by the lack of disease models. However, induced pluripotent stem cells are emerging as useful platforms for the study of the molecular mechanisms of the condition, including mtDNA variants as well as evaluating possible therapies.10 MCM is a complex, heterogeneous condition that may affect infants, children, and adults and is frequently overlooked. This diagnosis should be considered in patients with unexplained cardiomyopathy. Intensified examination of patients with this condition may uncover a deeper understanding of previously unrecognized mechanisms of myocardial dysfunction. There is much that we don’t know about this condition. There is a great need for development of pharmacotherapies which, if effective in MCM, might be beneficial in patients with other aetiologies of cardiac disease as well.

title: Intracoronary autologous bone marrow cell transfer after acute myocardial infarction: abort and refocus
abstract: This editorial refers to ‘Intracoronary autologous bone marrow cell transfer after myocardial infarction: the BOOST-2 randomised placebo-controlled clinical trial’†, by K.C. Wollert et al., on page 2936. Non sunt multiplicanda entia sine necessitate Johannes Poncius, 1639 commentary on the works of Duns Scotus Timely interventional coronary reperfusion is the single most important act that a cardiologist can perform to reverse dramatic consequences of the acutely occluded coronary artery associated with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Progress in the standard of care with shortening of the ischaemic times as well as adjunctive pharmacotherapy yielded a profound impact on survival, myocardial salvage, and quality of life.1 Nevertheless, despite timely reperfusion and global adoption of a 24/7 primary percutaneous coronary intervention (pPCI) service, the hospitalization rates for ischaemic cardiovascular events or heart failure still reach 14% with 6- to 12-month mortality rates ranging between 6% and 12%.1 , 2 In particular, patients with extensive post-infarct left ventricular (LV) dysfunction represent the population at risk, prone to develop overt heart failure, and could benefit from innovative strategies facilitating myocardial recovery. Any innovative approach aiming to facilitate myocardial recovery after acute ischaemic injury, such as autologous bone marrow cell (BMC) therapy, competes against improving standards of guideline-based therapies in STEMI patients, setting the bar high regarding the clinical impact and expectations if such a therapy were adopted. The current standard of care with widespread availability of pPCI, current drug-eluting stents, and antiplatelet medications, as well as high prescription of beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers, or aldosterone blockers, is clearly different as compared with the period of initial cell therapy trials 10–15 years ago. Unlike at that time, the risk of post-infarction heart failure is modified not only by reduced LV function but increasingly also by other factors such as ageing or co-morbidities. Overall, the adoption of cell therapy on top of the 2017 STEMI standard of care requires: (i) proof of efficacy on clinical endpoints or a clinically relevant surrogate; (ii) drug-like standardization of production and storage; (iii) understanding the mechanism of action; (iv) demonstration of periprocedural and long-term safety; and (v) approval by regulatory bodies throughout Europe.3 Also, several other questions about practical implementation should be asked. BMC therapy requires bone marrow harvesting and cell production, followed by a second coronary catheterization associated with prolonged hospital stay. Would physicians be confident to recommend the second catheterization? Would the payer agree to cover such therapy, even if it has increased the ejection fraction (EF) by 5%, without data on long-term outcomes? What else would be needed to approve the therapy? All these factors should be taken into account when evaluating the current stage of autologous BMC therapy after STEMI. Over the last 15 years, numerous phase I and II studies explored adult BMC therapies as a post-STEMI adjunct.4–9 The clinical translation has been supported by the notion that adult stem and progenitor cells participate in myocardial repair, as well as by early pre-clinical studies demonstrating the benefits on myocardial remodelling and function in various animal models.4 In contrast to initial enthusiasm sparked by early small studies, outcomes of controlled clinical trials were mixed and often disappointing.4–9 The BOOST programme was initiated under the leadership of the late Helmut Drexler 15 years ago with the first randomized study on cell therapy after STEMI.9 Using the state-of-the-art magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) evaluation and open-label design, initial results of BOOST showed an early significant improvement in LVEF after BMC therapy.8 Despite the later observations that the benefit on cardiac function wore off at long-term follow-up,9 Wollert and colleagues aimed to re-evaluate the therapeutic potential of nucleated BMCs on MRI-derived LVEF in a randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled study. Published in this issue,10 BOOST-2 has been designed as a randomized, multi-arm and double-blind placebo-controlled study addressing pertinent unknowns of the cell therapy. Importantly, the investigators used the broader population of total nucleated BMCs rather than the mononuclear fraction (MNC) as an active biologic. For the first time, they aimed to investigate the mechanism of action and address the dose dependency in the clinical setting. To decode the paracrine effect vs. other putative factors (clonogenic/transdifferentiation) of nucleated BMCs, the BOOST-2 investigators compared fully competent vs. γ-irradiated cells devoid of colony-forming unit capability. The cells were well characterized, with preserved functional potency as evidenced by relevant functional assays, and the standardized protocol of cell separation was identical to that in the initial BOOST trial (gelatine—polysuccinate density gradient sedimentation). Disappointingly, the trial failed to show an improvement in LVEF fraction and did not meet any other secondary MRI endpoints. Likewise, there was no signal of the efficacy of fully competent cells compared with γ-irradiated cells or signals of a dose-dependent effect. The negative outcome of such a well-designed trial is disappointing. However, as alluded to earlier, it should be placed into the perspective of similar trials testing adjunctive approaches in STEMI2 and the current landscape of advanced standard of care. It should also be noted that even in the very experienced centres actively pursuing this trial, the projected sample size could not be reached and the trial was stopped prematurely. Slow enrolment is another ‘silent’ warning that perhaps the clinical need, at least as reflected in clinical follow-up surveillance in the population selected by the BOOST-2 trial, is not as high as one expects from the reported morbidity/mortality statistics.1 , 2 It is consistent with the inclusion of the relatively low-risk population as reflected by a high proportion of patients with moderately reduced LVEF at baseline with low morbidity, heart failure progression, or implantable cardioverter defibrillator implantation at 6 months follow-up. The negative outcome of such a well-designed and rigorously executed study as BOOST-2 will undoubtedly diminish the enthusiasm of other investigators to continue similar studies. Overall, BOOST-2, as presented in this issue, is closing series of trials with MRI readouts with no benefits on cardiac structure and function in the STEMI setting. Perhaps the principle of Ockham’s razor should be accepted, favouring the simplest answer and avoiding multiplying the entities beyond necessity. The neutral results indeed converge to the conclusion that despite a strong biologic rationale, current BMC therapy may simply not be effective in STEMI, at least regarding improvement in cardiac function. Nevertheless, before making this call, we should follow the principles of scientific thoroughness and await the outcome of the European Commission-funded BAMI project.11 The BAMI project extends the rigorous translational and clinical REPAIR-AMI programme that yields standardized, functionally superior cell biologics as compared with other cell therapy trials with bone marrow-derived MNCs.5 , 12 The comparison of REPAIR-AMI/BAMI and BOOST-2 is difficult because the number of cells is greater (20.6 ± 7.7 × 108 nucleated cells) and BAMI includes patients with more depressed LV function. It is also tempting to speculate that use of a heparin-free cell production environment is superior based on the mechanistic studies on disrupted stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1)-mediated migration.12 Thus, the results of the BAMI trial are much awaited by the scientific community despite the delay in its initiation after promising 2006 results of the phase II REPAIR-AMI trial.5 BAMI findings and its deliverables are likely to provide the final call on intracoronary cell therapy as a biologic adjunct early after STEMI. How would late Helmut Drexler, as a thoughtful and forward-looking clinical scientist, act knowing the previous unknowns? The imperative of every negative setback is to refocus and redefine the next objectives and hypotheses. Cell therapy should be focusing on defining its place in multidisciplinary heart failure management including other emerging biologics or device-based approaches. If the cell therapy is to be adopted within the current armamentarium of standard of care, it should provide compelling translational and clinical evidence on myocardial repair halting the progression of LV dysfunction and heart failure3 , 13 (Figure 1). Expectations vs. evidence paving the way for adoption of stem cell therapy for cardiac repair. Intracoronary autologous bone marrow cell therapy fails to meet the initial expectations as an adjunct after STEMI. Refocusing on the clinical need in heart failure, next-generation reparative strategies are being built on the translational research programme with relevant biologics tested in the outcome-oriented clinical translation. Several translational and clinical research programmes are advancing the knowledge on mechanisms of action and strategies boosting the potency of reparative biologics. In this regard, the work of the BOOST investigators on the analysis of the proteome of BMCs and identification of potential regenerative paracrine factors should be applauded.14 They showcase an example of an acellular next-generation regenerative strategy. Other examples include next-generation products of expanded multicellular or lineage-specified products as well as bioengineered or combined approaches.3 , 13 , 15 Together with optimization of delivery strategies and definition of the optimal therapeutic window of the target population, they strive to boost reproducible and effective myocardial repair (Figure 1). Intracoronary cell therapy to date is not meeting the over-reaching expectations from the early 2000s. We should acknowledge that they were unrealistic and based on a too simplistic reasoning. The early clinical adoption demonstrated unequivocally the safety of cell therapy, dissipating the ethical dilemma of whether it was justified to embark on clinical studies with limited pre-clinical knowledge. At the same time, lack of evidence or meaningful efficacy signals is a clear indication to refocus. Refocus on the persisting clinical needs in heart failure and build on the stepping stones of rigorous translational research, and thereby foster the therapeutic consistency of the regenerative interventions. title: Magnetic resonance imaging-based ID of the vasculature across the heart–brain axis
abstract: Failure of the microvasculature is increasingly moving into the spotlight as a new frontier in cardiovascular medicine, underpinning many of today’s most burdening diseases.1 However, a paucity of tools for its non-invasive characterization critically limits our understanding of microvascular diseases. The European Research Council (ERC) has awarded a Start-up Grant to pursue closing this gap. In the VascularID project, researchers from the TU Delft are tasked with the development, validation, and demonstration of novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based tools to quantitatively uncover microvascular properties in vivo. The microvasculature describes the network of small vessels throughout the body, comprising arterioles, venules, and capillaries. While significant progress has been made in the diagnosis and treatment of ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke caused by the occlusion of large arteries, many diseases of the microvasculature remain an open clinical question. About 20%–60% of ischaemic heart disease, stroke, and dementia cases are caused by small vessel disease.1,2 Cardiovascular disease entities that are thought to be related to microvascular dysfunction, include heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, myocardial infarct/ischaemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries, or Takatsubo (Figure 1). Pathologies of the microvasculature in the brain are described as cerebral small vessel disease and constitute one of the major contributors to vascular cognitive dementia and cognitive decline in the elderly. These cardio- and cerebrovascular diseases often present together and are linked to common comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, obesity, or aging.2 Microvascular rarefaction is a common feature of these comorbidities and is known to precede the onset of symptoms.3 Thus, the microvasculature is increasingly moving into the focus of cardiovascular research and takes centre stage in the search for the link, explaining the connection between disease entities of the heart and the brain (the heart–brain axis).4 Impairment of the microvasculature is a hallmark of many of today’s most burdening diseases across the heart–brain axis, including forms of ischaemic heart disease, stroke, and dementia. The lack of early, non-invasive markers limits our pathophysiological understanding and crucially affects treatment success, as preventive intervention is the only successful clinical management strategy available. Our understanding of the (patho)physiology has always been intimately linked to the availability of tools for its observation, dating back all the way to Antoni van Leeuwenhoek’s account of the red blood cells in the latter half of the 17th century. For example, occlusion of large arteries can be directly visualized with various medical imaging modalities. Ischaemic events in the heart or the brain that result from these occlusions are well characterized and understood, their diagnosis is reliable and treatment options are plentiful. With diameters down to <10 μm, large parts of the microvasculature escape direct detection with current medical imaging technology, due to limitations in the attainable imaging resolution. Thus, to date, a comprehensive assessment of the microvasculature can only be achieved with histology. In vivo, this requires an invasive sample biopsy, which can rarely be obtained. The lack of non-invasive tools greatly hinders our understanding of the pathophysiology and consequently limits the treatment options for microvascular disease after the onset of symptoms.4 Early interventions, including preventive lifestyle changes, present a central strategy for clinical management, but a lack of early disease markers hampers patient selection for the best treatment and evaluation of interventions. Comprehensive non-invasive characterization of the microvasculature is needed to advance therapeutic developments and facilitate selective, preventive interventions. Magnetic resonance imaging is a mainstay in clinical radiology and is gaining an increasing foothold in cardiovascular medicine in recent years.5 While its imaging resolution remains limited compared with CT, the strength of MRI lies in the unparalleled, wide spectrum of contrast information. Physical phenomena from the nano- to the macroscopic scale contribute to the signal strength in MRI and give rise to a plethora of imaging contrasts enabling in-depth tissue characterization. As a result, MRI can depict a macroscopic ensemble average of microscopic phenomena. Clinically established examples include the measurement of microscopic displacement in diffusion MRI or the indirect detection of macromolecules in chemical exchange saturation transfer. Another rich source of contrast has been found in the susceptibility difference between deoxygenated blood and surrounding tissue. First described as the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) effect by Ogawa et al.,6 BOLD became widely used in a range of MRI applications. Most notably functional MRI (fMRI) uses the BOLD effect to detect neural activity. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is also increasingly gaining attention for the visualization of mesoscopic vessels in MRI.7 Seminal research has been carried out modelling the susceptibility fields around the microvasculature to quantitatively describe their contributions to the MRI signal and the BOLD effect.8,9 Such models enabled a validated estimation of the blood oxygen extraction fraction and the venous blood volume. In combination with exogenous contrast agents, this has been shown to allow for the estimation of a blood-volume weighted vessel size average.10 These techniques are examples of the promising window that susceptibility effects provide in uncovering microvascular properties in vivo. The VascularID project builds a research line to explore the potential of susceptibility effects for quantitative assessment of microvascular properties across the heart–brain axis (Figure 2). In this research programme, researchers from the TU Delft aim to develop new approaches to leverage the susceptibility fields created in microvascular vessel networks and derive quantitative imaging biomarkers for the use of cardio- and cerebrovascular diseases. Existing and novel MRI techniques will be combined in an attempt to provide an imaging suite for a comprehensive assessment of the microvasculature. Thorough investigation and metrological characterization of those imaging biomarkers will be pursued. State-of-the-art microprinting will be used to generate well-controlled environments of characteristic susceptibility fields to validate the physical signal models. Animal models allow for in vivo validation against whole organ histology and can shed unique light on the biological sensitivity of the imaging biomarkers. Inching towards clinical qualification, comprehensive testing in healthy subjects, and demonstration of clinical feasibility in relevant patient populations across the heart–brain axis will fortify the imaging toolbox for large-scale evaluation in the clinic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has an imaging resolution multiple orders of magnitude larger than the size of the microvasculature. Nonetheless, physical interactions of the hydrogen nuclei constituting the source of the magnetic resonance imaging signal can unlock comprehensive characterization of the microvascular vessel network across the heart–brain axis in vivo. This figure has been designed using assets from Freepik.com. Continuous advances in MR imaging physics and technology have put us in a position to exploit the subtle characteristics of microvascular susceptibility fields in vivo. This may provide a seminal approach toward the characterization of microvascular diseases. Supported by an ERC Start-Up grant this project attempts to provide new tools for the study of microvascular pathophysiological processes. At a time when microvascular diseases emerge as a new frontier in cardiovascular medicine, it may equip cardiovascular researchers and practitioners with the much-needed tools to take on one of the major healthcare challenges of our time. No new data were generated or analysed in support of this research. title: Emerging fields for therapeutic targeting of the aldosterone–mineralocorticoid receptor signaling pathway
abstract: This article is part of a themed issue on Emerging Fields for Therapeutic Targeting of the Aldosterone-Mineralocorticoid Receptor Signaling Pathway. To view the other articles in this section visit http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bph.v179.13/issuetoc The physiological role of aldosterone is to control salt-water homeostasis by acting on the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in renal epithelial cells (Jaisser & Farman, 2016). By increasing the expression of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and Na+/K+-ATPase, aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and fluid retention (Jaisser & Farman, 2016). Besides this physiological function, the MR takes an important role in disease. At the turn of the 21st century, large clinical trials such as the Randomized Aldactone Evaluation Study (RALES) demonstrated a striking benefit of treatment with MR antagonists in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (Pitt et al., 1999). These findings triggered enormous research activity during the past few years that substantially advanced our understanding of the molecular, cellular, and pathophysiological functions of the MR. The present issue summarizes the current knowledge of the aldosterone-MR signaling pathway, from molecular biology to clinical application, with a focus on potential new indications and novel strategies for pharmacological targeting (Figure 1). The MR is a ligand-activated transcription factor that, together with the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) and others, belongs to the nuclear receptor superfamily. Upon binding of aldosterone or cortisol, the MR shuttles from the cytosol to the nucleus and directly interacts with the chromatin. In their review article on the molecular function of the MR, Grossmann et al. (2022) provide a comprehensive overview of how structure, posttranslational modifications, or interaction with cofactors determine MR activity and distinguish it from the GR and other nuclear receptors, forming the basis for the experimental and translational studies to follow. Bauersachs and Lopez-Andres (2022) review the role of the MR in cardiovascular disease. Based on the established benefits of MR antagonists in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, they have been evaluated in clinical trials for the treatment of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, acute heart failure, or postmyocardial infarction remodeling. Numerous experimental models have been applied to test MR antagonists in potential new indications beyond heart failure such as heart valve disease or pulmonary hypertension. Gene targeting in mice allows dissection of the impact of the MR in different cell types on cardiovascular remodeling or blood pressure control and to distinguish them from the MR in renal epithelial cells (Bauersachs & Lopez-Andres, 2022). Several experimental studies have demonstrated the pivotal importance of the MR in cells of the innate and adaptive immune system for cardiovascular disease (van der Heijden et al., 2022). Intriguingly, aldosterone by acting on the MR can induce long-lasting pro-inflammatory effects in macrophages in the sense of trained immunity. This suggests that the MR might not only play a role in acute inflammatory processes such as myocardial infarction but also chronic low-grade inflammatory conditions including atherosclerosis or arterial hypertension (van der Heijden et al., 2022). Importantly, MR-related inflammation is not restricted to the cardiovascular system. In the kidney, MR activation in vascular cells, immune cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, or fibroblasts induces tissue inflammation that is associated with increased oxidative stress, extracellular matrix production, and functional deterioration (Barrera-Chimal et al., 2022). Barrera-Chimal et al. (2022) summarize insights derived from numerous experimental and clinical studies exploring the potential of MR antagonists in kidney disease from different causes and the molecular mechanisms involved. The pivotal role of the MR in diabetes and metabolic syndrome has recently been highlighted by the FIDELIO-DKD study, a large phase 3 clinical trial demonstrating beneficial effects of finerenone versus placebo on renal outcomes in patients with diabetic kidney disease (Bakris et al., 2020). During the past few years, there has been increasing evidence that the MR is of pathophysiological importance in a variety of additional organ systems, including the eye, liver, skin, or brain (Figure 1a). Thus, it seems worthwhile to evaluate whether the findings obtained on the MR in heart and kidney diseases can be transferred to other conditions, potentially leading to the repurposing of MR antagonists for new indications. Non-alcoholic liver disease is highly prevalent and one of the major causes of liver cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Advanced liver cirrhosis is often associated with hyperaldosteronism and MR antagonists are in routine clinical use to improve portal hypertension (Schreier et al., 2022). Data from experimental studies suggest a broader role for the MR, showing beneficial effects of MR blockade on liver metabolic function, inflammation, and cirrhosis. Interestingly, MR deletion from myeloid cells, including Kupffer cells, improved liver inflammation in mice, suggesting similar mechanisms involved as have been observed in the cardiovascular system (Schreier et al., 2022). A growing body of evidence indicates that the MR modulates both physiological and pathological processes in skin homeostasis and disease. In the skin, the MR is co-expressed with the GR and molecular studies including chromatin immunoprecipitation suggest that they mutually influence each other and have at least partially overlapping functions (Perez, 2022). Glucocorticoids are standard of care and widely used for many inflammatory cutaneous disorders, however, high doses or long-term treatment may cause skin atrophy, increased fragility, and impaired wound healing. Intriguingly, these adverse effects could be attenuated by local MR blockade. Specific formulations may improve skin permeability of MR antagonists, enabling dermatological use. Of note, MR deletion from keratinocytes was reported to exacerbate the response to inflammatory stimuli in mice (Perez, 2022). This is in contrast to the clear pro-inflammatory role of the MR in other organs and indicates that the safety and efficacy of MR blockade require careful evaluation depending on the pathophysiological context. Oxidative stress, oedema, inflammation, and neovascularization are key features of retinal diseases that represent the most common causes of blindness worldwide. In their review article, Behar-Cohen and Zhao (2022) put together what is known about the consequences of MR activation or inhibition in retinal disease. The current evidence derived from experimental studies suggests beneficial effects of MR antagonists or cell-selective MR gene targeting in mice, involving epithelial cells, neurons, microglia, and endothelial cells of the retina and the choroid. Challenges for the clinical use of MR antagonists in retinal diseases remain as available steroidal compounds do not cross the blood-retinal barrier (Behar-Cohen & Zhao, 2022). The MR is highly expressed in the brain, particularly in neurons of the hippocampus, and affects emotional and cognitive functions in both, mental health and disease, including major depressive disorder or borderline personality disorder (Paul et al., 2022). Notably, glucocorticoids are the main ligands for the MR and GR in the brain, which causes a close interaction of MR signaling with the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. In this issue, Paul et al. (2022) decipher MR functions in the brain, step by step from basal molecular mechanisms to animal models and clinical studies, highlighting the imbalance of MR and GR signaling as a key pathophysiological mechanism. The use of currently available steroidal MR antagonists, spironolactone or eplerenone, is limited by adverse effects related to inhibition of the MR in epithelial cells, foremost hyperkalemia. This has led to the development of several new, nonsteroidal MR antagonists during the past decade, including esaxerenone, AZD9977, apararenone, KBP-5074, and finerenone. Kintscher et al. (2022) review the pharmacological and molecular properties of these novel compounds and delineate their course of development through the different stages. They discuss in detail the clinical trials of esaxerenone and finerenone, which were recently approved for arterial hypertension or diabetic kidney disease, respectively, and have entered clinical use (Kintscher et al., 2022). The advances in our understanding of its molecular and pathophysiological function summarized in this issue provide new and innovative approaches for targeting the MR signaling pathway. However, a better understanding of the exact spatial, temporal, and cellular contributions of the MR to the diseases discussed in this issue is still needed. Presently used MR antagonists inhibit the MR in all tissues resulting in unwanted side effects. Cell and tissue-specific antagonists have to be developed that work differently from classical ligand-receptor binding, inhibiting nuclear receptor activity by modulation of cell type-specific co-regulator interactions (Clarisse et al., 2022). Finerenone, as a proof of principle, modifies MR nuclear shuttling and the recruitment of MR co-regulators (Kintscher et al., 2022). Potential other approaches include drugs with preferential uptake in target cells or organs, local delivery systems, inhibition of MR downstream effector molecules, epigenetic inhibitors, or RNA-based antisense therapies (Clarisse et al., 2022). The recent clinical success of nonsteroidal MR antagonists has sparked a renewed interest in the MR and motivated scientists to evaluate the role of the MR in various diseases. To advance new therapeutic approaches will require the collaboration of scientists from different disciplines and backgrounds, spanning the full spectrum of basic, translational, and clinical research. We hope that this themed issue will further spur readers' interest in MR research and help to unravel the many secrets that the MR still holds for us. title: From epicardial coronary arteries to the coronary microcirculation: novel insights into a neglected issue
abstract: Alterations in the structure and function of large epicardial coronary arteries remain the most important causes of morbidity and mortality in most countries.1 While cardiologists focus on the angiographically visible part of the coronary circulation because it is easy accessible by current imaging modalities2 and interventional and surgical techniques, the microcirculation has been largely neglected. There are good reasons to focus future research efforts on the microcirculation. First, patients with a clinical presentation of an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and non-obstructive coronary artery disease have almost as bad an outcome as those with ‘classical’ ACS. Secondly, non-obstructive coronary atherosclerosis is observed in up to 50% of patients with angina and positive stress test results undergoing diagnostic coronary angiography. Thirdly, Tako Tsubo syndrome has been recognized as a microcirculatory ACS. These aspects are further expanded in a Current Opinion ‘The parallel tales of microvascular angina and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a paradigm shift’, by Filippo Crea and colleagues from the Universita Cattolica del Santo Cuore in Romy, Italy,3 which reiterates that the prevalence of microvascular angina is higher than previously thought and associated with worse clinical outcomes than those observed in asymptomatic subjects with a similar risk factor burden. The authors remind us that the diagnosis of microvascular angina is based on: (i) symptoms of myocardial ischaemia; (ii) absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease; (iii) evidence of myocardial ischaemia on non-invasive stress testing; and (iv) evidence of impaired coronary microvascular function. The clinical relevance of microvascular angina has been overlooked since the diagnostic tools for the evaluation of the microcirculation are infrequently utilized. A parallel ‘tale’ could be proposed for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, which the authors subsequently elaborate on to present a provocative hypothesis on the potential role of the microcirculation in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. In a review entitled ‘Coronary microcirculatory pathophysiology: can we afford it to remain a black box?’ Axel R. Pries and colleagues from the Charité in Berlin, Germany further discuss this issue and note that coronary microvascular networks indeed play a key role in determining blood flow distribution in the myocardium.4 Matching local blood supply to tissue metabolic demand entails continuous adaptation of coronary vessels via regulation of smooth muscle tone and structural adaptations. Despite an increasing number of clinical studies demonstrating the importance of microcirculatory dysfunction in collateral formation,5 ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction,6 and microvascular obstruction,7 as well as certain forms of angina and heart failure as outlined above, overall the knowledge on the mechanisms involved and cause–effect relationships is still very limited. Numerous pathophysiological hypotheses for microvascular angina and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction have been suggested, but are not established to a sufficient degree to allow a clinically useful definition of nosological entities, stratification of affected patients, or the development of effective therapeutic strategies. The authors suggest that this may be at least in part related to a steep decline in experimental animal studies in this area. The microvascular pathophysiology can only be investigated in the beating heart. The authors propose to use a concerted effort of ‘Coronary Microvascular Observatories’ to close this knowledge gap and to accelerate clinical progress in this area. Study flowchart. VSA, vasospastic angina; CMD, coronary microvascular dysfunction; MLP, myocardial lactate production. (from Odaka Y, Takahashi J, Tsuburaya R, Nishimiya K, Hao K, Matsumoto Y, Ito K, Sakata Y, Miyata S, Manita D, Hirowatari Y, Shimokawa H. Plasma concentration of serotonin is a novel biomarker for coronary microvascular dysfunction in patients with suspected angina and unobstructive coronary arteries. See pages 489--496.) Traditional prognostic risk assessment in patients undergoing non-invasive imaging is based on a limited selection of clinical risk scores11 and imaging findings.12 Machine learning can consider a greater number and complexity of variables, a concept that has been applied to the diagnosis of ‘classical’ coronary artery disease by Piotr Slomka and colleagues from the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, California in their clinical research paper entitled ‘Machine learning for prediction of all-cause mortality in patients with suspected coronary artery disease: a 5-year multicentre prospective registry analysis’. They investigated the feasibility and accuracy of machine learning to predict 5-year all-cause mortality in 10 030 patients undergoing coronary computed tomographic angiography or CCTA, and compared the performance with existing clinical or CCTA metrics.13 A total of 25 clinical and 44 CCTA parameters were evaluated, including segment stenosis score, segment involvement score, modified Duke index, number of segments with non-calcified, mixed, or calcified plaques, age, sex, gender, standard cardiovascular risk factors, and Framingham risk score. Machine learning involved automated feature selection by information gain ranking, model building with a boosted ensemble algorithm, and 10-fold stratified cross-validation. Overall, 745 patients died during 5-year follow-up. Machine learning exhibited a higher area under the curve (AUC) compared with the Framingham risk score or CCTA severity scores alone for predicting all-cause mortality. The authors conclude that machine learning combining clinical and CCTA data predicted 5-year all-cause mortality better than existing clinical or CCTA metrics alone. These provocative findings are critically discussed in an Editorial by Paul Schoenhagen from the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, USA.14 Besides imaging and current cardiovascular risk factors, microRNAs have emerged as novel biomarkers.15,16 Better risk stratification for future coronary events is of considerable interest because of the potential to guide secondary preventive therapies, particularly with the advent of highly effective, but expensive PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitors. In a Basic Science article entitled ‘Circulating microRNAs strongly predict cardiovascular death in patients with coronary artery disease: results from the large AtheroGene Study’, Tanja Zeller and colleagues from the University Heart Center Hamburg in Germany addressed this issue.17 The serum concentrations of eight candidate microRNAs, miR-19a, miR-19b, miR-132, miR-140-3p, miR-14-5p, miR-150, miR-186, and miR-210, were measured in a cohort of 1112 patients with documented coronary artery disease, including 430 patients with ACS and 682 patients with stable angina pectoris. Cardiovascular death was the main outcome measure. During a median follow-up of 4.0 years, most microRNAs reliably predicted cardiovascular death in ACS patients. Cox regression analyses indicated that per one standard deviation increase of, in particular, miR-132 with a hazard ratio of 2.85, miR-140-3p with a hazard ratio of 2.88, and miR-210 with a hazard ratio of 3.10 precisely predicted cardiovascular death. Circulating miR-132, mIR-140-3p, and miR-210 clearly improved various model performance measures, including C-statistics. The authors conclude that this, the largest study so far in evaluating the prognostic value of circulating miRNAs, shows that single miRNAs derived from peripheral blood predict mortality in secondary prevention settings, and thereby represent valuable biomarkers for risk estimation in coronary artery disease. The potential value of these findings is evaluated in an interesting Editorial by Christian Weber from the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität in Munich, Germany.18 In a complementary study, albeit with a case–control approach, corroborating the prognostic value of microRNAs after ACS, Jakob et al. from the Charité in Berlin and the Center for Molecular Cardiology in Zurich evaluated in their Brief Communication ‘Profiling and validation of circulating microRNAs for cardiovascular events in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction’ based on a multicentre, prospective ACS cohort with 1002 out of 2168 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction or STEMI presented similar results. Sixty-three STEMI patients experienced an adjudicated major cardiovascular event or MACE as defined as cardiac death or recurrent myocardial infarction within 1 year.19 From a microRNA profiling in a matched derivation case–control cohort, 14 microRNAs were selected for validation. Comparing 63 cases vs. 126 controls, three microRNAs were significantly differentially abundant in patients with MACE: while miR-26b-5p levels were decreased, those of miR-320a (and miR-660-5p) were increased. miR-26b-5p has been suggested to prevent adverse cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, whereas miR-320a promotes cardiomyocyte death and apoptosis, and miR-660-5p has been related to active platelet production. This suggests that miR-26b-5p, miR-320a, and miR-660-5p may reflect alterations of different pathophysiological pathways involved in clinical outcome after ACS. Consistently, these three microRNAs reliably discriminated cases from controls in an age- and sex-adjusted Cox regression for miR-26b-5p, miR-660-5p, and miR-320a. The combination of these three microRNAs further increased the AUC. Importantly, addition of these three microRNAs to both the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) score and a clinical model increased AUC further from 0.679 to 0.720 and 0.722 to 0.732, respectively, with a net reclassification improvement of 0.20 in both cases. These findings suggest that the release of specific microRNAs into the circulation may reflect the activation of molecular pathways that impact on clinical outcome after STEMI. The editors hope that this issue of the European Heart Journal will be of interest to its readers.

title: Bridging the Gap between Translational and Outcome Research in Cardiovascular Disease
abstract:
The adjective “translational” stems from Ancient Latin “translatio” (transfero, carry over). Translational research is the branch of scientific research aimed at transferring discoveries obtained in basic research investigations to the clinical context. Accordingly, in the field of biomedical sciences the concept of translational research relates to the transfer of scientific knowledge into practical clinical applications in order to improve the management and treatment of human diseases.

Medicine in general is particularly fascinated by the translational concept, probably for its peculiar applied scopes, and cardiology is not an exception. In this regard, the International Society for Cardiovascular Translational Research (http://www.isctr.org/) was founded in 2007 with the objective to coordinate and guide basic and clinical researchers, regulatory authorities, and the medical industry to improve the process of transferring new scientific evidence into clinical applications, promote translational research and divulgate new scientific results to the scientific community, and develop guidelines for conducting translational research studies. In addition, the ISCTR and the American College of Cardiology (ACC) collaborative efforts began in 2010 involving education on translational science pathways.

The reason behind the interest for translation research in the cardiovascular field is obvious. Although huge advances in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases have been made during the last decades, the morbidity and mortality associated with heart diseases are still too high [1]. In particular, the incidence of heart failure continues to increase with a progressively higher overload for national health systems and health care providers involved in the management of this chronic and highly disabling disease. For all these reasons, it is crucial to develop new therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of cardiac diseases, with a particular focus on heart failure. However, the only way to be successful in this difficult task is to implement the efforts devoted to translational research.

One important goal of cardiovascular translational research is the discovery of new biomarkers that could be useful for the diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and therapeutic management of specific cardiac diseases [2]. This can be achieved by testing whether factors, which were previously found to be associated with specific cardiovascular disease models in experimental studies, are indeed useful for the clinical management of patients affected by these illnesses. These biomarkers could be circulating humoral factors or specific cellular subtypes, or preclinical markers of organ damage. For example, it is now well established that a reduction of flow-mediated artery dilation in human subjects is a preclinical sign of endothelial dysfunction and an independent predictor of adverse cardiovascular events [3].

Another important interest of translational research is the elucidation of the genetic basis of cardiovascular diseases. In fact, the clarification of the genetic predisposition to cardiovascular illnesses can help to identify those subjects who need a different clinical management. Genome-wide association studies are continuously providing new insights into the gene variants associated with cardiovascular sicknesses [4]. However, case-cohort studies or longitudinal investigations are also brilliantly identifying new polymorphisms linked to an increased incidence of cardiovascular diseases or to a worse prognosis. For example, recent studies demonstrated that T2238C atrial natriuretic peptide gene variant is independently associated with an increased incidence of adverse cardiovascular events [5].

A fundamental field in cardiovascular research is also represented by the study of cardioprotection [6]. In fact, the discovery of new therapies reducing the amount of myocardial death during an acute myocardial infarction would help to significantly reduce the incidence of subsequent cardiac dysfunction and heart failure. This would be possible only if the mechanisms regulating cardiomyocyte survival and death during myocardial ischemia are elucidated so that appropriate therapeutic targets can be identified. Unfortunately, in the last decades only few of the therapeutic interventions effective in the reduction of myocardial infarction and cardiac remodeling in animal models of ischemia, ischemia/reperfusion, and chronic myocardial infarction resulted to be effective also in patients experiencing a real heart attack. This may be due to the fact that the animal models of myocardial ischemia and infarction currently employed in basic experimental studies do not accurately mimic the pathophysiology of a human myocardial infarction [7]. Future efforts of researchers working on cardioprotection should be devoted to the development of more relevant models of cardiac diseases.

Finally, a fascinating and promising field of translational research is represented by cardiac regeneration. The possibility for physicians to repair a failing heart with stem cells or applied tissue-engineered myocardial patches still represents a new frontier for the treatment of heart failure [8]. Unfortunately, as in the field of cardioprotection, most of the attempts to effectively translate the highly promising experimental results obtained in this field into the clinical setting highlighted mixed results with benefits ranging from absent to transient or, at most, marginal [9, 10]. A part of the delay in the therapeutic advancement in the field of stem cells and cardiac regeneration is caused by the fact that little is still known about the mechanisms to increase stem cell survival after in vivo transplantation and to efficiently induce its transdifferentiation into mature cardiomyocytes. These mechanisms need to be urgently elucidated in future investigations. In addition, the standardization of the procedures for isolation, purification, manipulation, and transplantation of human stem cells used for therapeutic purposes needs to be implemented, despite the fact that the standards of safety and quality for stem cell therapeutic uses are currently defined in the Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) guidelines (see Eudralex EU guidelines for Good Manufacturing Practice for Medicinal Products for Human and Veterinary Use) [11, 12]. Nonetheless, full compliance with GMP is a mandatory aspect of stem cell-tissue engineering and manufacturing.

The improvement of translational research, however, cannot represent alone the solution for developing new strategies for the cure of cardiovascular diseases. Together with translational research, it would be highly important to implement also clinical and outcome research. These scientific research branches aim to further expand the current knowledge of the prevalence, incidence, impact, and management of cardiovascular abnormal conditions in selected or real-world patients. This would help to identify shortfalls in practice and to develop strategies to improve care. In particular, outcome research is planned to continuously provide new insights into the therapeutic interventions working best for specific types of patients and under specific circumstances.

Given these premises, this special issue aimed at integrating expertise from different disciplines toward the same objective: a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying cardiovascular diseases as well as the development of new therapeutic strategies to prevent or treat cardiovascular diseases. In our opinion the result was notable. Among the accepted manuscripts, some studies developed new methods enhancing the cardiovascular transdifferentiation of stem cells or standardized the procedures for the isolation of bone marrow-derived cellular subtypes for the treatment of refractory ischemia. Other manuscripts dealt with the molecular mechanisms underlying ischemia/reperfusion damage or heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The biomarkers associated with resistant hypertension or aortic aneurism rupture were also studied. In addition, some epidemiologic studies provided new insights into the factors associated with coronary artery disease or with a worse cardiovascular outcome. Finally, the genetic basis of metabolically unhealthy obesity was also investigated.

The editors really hope that the scientific contributions accepted for this special issue may contribute in some extent to the advance of the current knowledge of the pathophysiology, prognosis, and management of cardiovascular diseases.

title: Cardiac Beta3-Adrenergic Receptors in the Clinical Arena: The End of the Beginning
abstract: This article refers to ‘The first-in-man randomized trial of a beta3 adrenoceptor agonist in chronic heart failure: the BEAT-HF trial’, by H. Bundgaard et al., published in this issue on pages 566–575. Despite significant advances in treatment options, heart failure remains a devastating disease with significant morbidity/mortality and economic burden. In this context, new therapeutic approaches are eagerly needed. The paper by Bundgaard in this issue of the journal1 proposes a treatment target, the third isotype of beta-adrenergic receptors (β3 AR) that was identified in the human myocardium >15 years ago,2 but only recently tested in the clinical arena thanks to the availability of a specific agonist, mirabegron. The molecule is available for clinical use in urology for the treatment of overactive bladder disease, a painful condition of frequent micturition, based on its well-established relaxing effect on the bladder smooth muscle that expresses β3 AR.3 Bundgaard et al. now present the results of a first pilot trial of mirabegron in patients suffering from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the rationale of which was based on pre-clinical data pointing to beneficial effects of β3 AR activation in the failing myocardium. Although the trial did not meet its primary endpoint (increase in LVEF over placebo), a non-pre-specified, subgroup analysis in patients with the lowest EF suggests potential benefits in subjects with more severe LV dysfunction. β3 ARs are clearly different from the two other well-known isotypes of β AR. In contrast to β1 and β2 ARs, their expression increases in the diseased myocardium2 and they are resistant to desensitization.4 i.e. they remain coupled to intracellular downstream signalling and maintain their effect in the presence of high concentrations of catecholamines. This already makes them rather attractive targets in the setting of heart failure. Their coupling and effects on rhythm and contractility also contrast with classical β1 and β2 adrenergic responses. In human ventricular biopsies in organ baths,2, 5 but also in non-failing ventricular tissue from mice with cardiac-specific expression of the human β3 AR,6 high concentrations of agonists induce a decrease of unloaded contractile shortening. A similar slight negative inotropic effect was also observed by Bundgaard and colleagues after administration of β3 AR agonists in non-failing sheep in vivo.7 However, the effect was exactly the opposite, i.e. an increase of LV contractility by activating β3 ARs in sheep with heart failure.7 Admittedly, others have found discordant results with β3 AR modulation in other animal models8 that would contradict the proposition of Bundgaard and collaborators. Their merit was to test the hypothesis in a pilot human trial. They also built upon solid pre-clinical data supporting protective effects of β3 ARs on the myocardium. Mechanistically, β3 ARs couple to activation of nitric oxide synthases (NOSs) in rodent and human myocardium;5, 9 the resulting increase in cGMP and cGMP-dependent protein kinase I (cGKI) activation in part explains the attenuation of excitation–contraction coupling and contractility in the normal cardiac cell, but also the protection in failing myocytes; cGKI acts on at least three different targets to attenuate hypertrophic remodelling,10 but also activates protein phosphatase 2A to decrease NADPH oxidase activation, thereby decreasing reactive oxygen species production. In the authors' hypothesis, this antioxidant effect attenuates the oxidative inactivation of the Na+–K+-ATPase pump, thereby restoring the pump activity.11 This, in turn, reduces intracellular Na in cardiac myocytes. The authors reasoned that, in non-failing myocytes, this decrease in Na would attenuate Ca transients and reduce contractility. However, in failing myocytes with Na overload, restoration of the pump activity would reduce the excess intracellular Na and restore excitation-contraction coupling and contractility.7 This was the rationale to test mirabegron (a β3 AR agonist) in HFrEF. In the present pilot human trial, they randomized patients with HFrEF under standard therapy to either mirabegron or placebo for 6 months; although the current recommended dose for the urological indication is 50 mg/day, the protocol included a dose escalation up to 300 mg/day, which was attained in >90% of the patients. Notably, all patients had to be treated with beta-blockers per protocol before inclusion (the majority received carvedilol or metoprolol, at >75% of recommended target doses in both arms), which probably protected those in the active treatment arm from off-target effects of mirabegron (i.e. agonism at β1 and β2 ARs) at such high doses. Also, none of the patients was treated with digoxin (which would have obliterated the expected beneficial effect of mirabegron through Na+–K+-ATPase activation). Patients were screened by echocardiography and included on the basis of LVEF <40%. Although this underestimated LVEF, as measured by cardiac computed tomography (CT) at enrolment, both sample size calculation and measurement of the primary endpoint (LVEF before/after treatment) were done by cardiac CT. Nevertheless, most of the patients had moderate HFrEF (EF 38 ± 17% by CT) with >95% at NYHA class II. The aetiology of heart failure was ischaemia in ∼50% in both arms, and all were in sinus rhythm. The trial was powered to detect a change of 4% LVEF by CT. The primary endpoint (increase in LVEF by CT after 6 months) was not reached. Perhaps this is not unexpected, given the relatively mild starting LV dysfunction, consistent with other functional and biological parameters (6-min walk test, VO2 max, and NT-proBNP), making it a challenge for any additional drug to improve LV function further over standard therapy. In an exploratory subgroup analysis of patients with baseline CT LVEF <40%, eight patients under mirabegron improved LVEF from baseline to follow-up [mean difference: 5.9% (0.4–11.4%); P = 0.025], while 17 patients under placebo showed no significant change [mean difference: 0.4% (−2.2 to 2.9%); P = 0.88]. Although the numbers are too small for a definitive mechanistic explanation, this increase in LVEF seemed to be due mostly to a decrease in systolic volumes, while there was no change (i.e. further decrease) in heart rate (as expected under full background β1–2 blockade). Based on their mechanistic hypothesis and these preliminary results, the authors expect a higher benefit of the β3 AR agonist in patients with more severe LV dysfunction. However, one may question such a simple conclusion. First, the endpoint chosen here, LVEF, may not be the best predictor of outcome in HF patients, and it remains to be demonstrated that the (modest) increase in LVEF translates into clinical (i.e. morbidity, other functional parameters, mortality) benefit. Interventional trials with positive inotropic drugs have mostly failed to demonstrate improved survival.12 Nevertheless, β3 AR agonists may confer benefits through other effects on LV remodelling that may be revealed in other trials with more mechanistic endpoints. Indeed, β3 ARs are expressed not only in cardiac myocytes, but also in endothelial cells of the human coronary vasculature, where they mediate both nitric oxide-dependent and independent relaxations that persist in coronary resistance vessels from diseased patients.13 In the remodelling myocardium, this would contribute to maintain coronary perfusion and avoid further ischaemic damage. In animal models, activation of β3 ARs on cardiac myocytes also attenuates hypertrophic remodelling and fibrosis in response to neurohormonal stress or haemodynamic overload.9 In combination, these effects may prevent adverse myocardial remodelling and improve not only systolic but also diastolic function. Such parameters were not evaluated in the BEAT-HF trial, but are being studied in a multicentre European trial on the effect of mirabegron in patients with structural heart disease (stage B) with, or at risk of developing heart failure with preserved EF (ISRCTN 65055502). Of note, a reduction of intracellular Na overload, as proposed through β3 AR activation, would also be beneficial in the context of diastolic dysfunction.14 Also, the combination of β3 AR agonists with β1 AR blockers, which seemed to be well tolerated in the present pilot trial, may be particularly suited given previous evidence for a mutual potentiation on downstream NOS/cGMP signaling.15 Finally, activation of β3 AR may confer indirect cardiovascular benefits through activation of extracardiac targets, e.g. on beige/brown fat, and subsequent improvements in peripheral metabolism and insulin sensitivity.16 Whether any or all of these effects will translate into clinically measurable variables and improved outcome will need to be confirmed from the results of trials ongoing or yet to come. In this respect, it is good news that the authors of the BEAT-HF trial decided to launch a larger, more mechanistic trial in HFrEF, while the Beta3lvh trial is exploring more long-term effects on remodelling, endothelial function, and metabolism. At the very least, the BEAT-HF trial demonstrated very few or no side effects (under full β1–β2 AR blockade) in HFrEF patients, which is also reassuring for those patients currently taking the drug for urological indications. title: Strain as hallmark to prevent interruption of breast cancer therapy
abstract: This editorial refers to ‘Strain-oriented strategy for guiding cardioprotection initiation of breast cancer patients experiencing cardiac dysfunction’ by C. Santoro et al., pp. 1345--1352. As cancer progression-free survival is continuously improving with new and evolving oncology therapies, short- and long-term off-target cardiovascular effects gain crucial importance for overall outcome.1 Chemo-, immuno-, radiation-, and targeted-therapies not only effect the malignant neoplastic cells, but also cardiomyocytes and vascular cells, leading to asymptomatic cardiac impairment up to overt severe heart failure or even fulminant myocarditis.2 The ideal method of early detection of cardiotoxicity in patients undergoing oncology regimens, and when to initiate preventive cardiac medication in cardiotoxicity in order to avoid acute or long-term heart failure development remains controversial. On the other hand, cardiac drugs may aggravate hypotension, hyperkalaemia, or renal function in patients with chemotherapy, e.g. emesis, and therefore, an immediate concomitant cardiac therapy is not established currently and needs further research. Echocardiography plays a pivotal role with monitoring of the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in 2D- or better 3D technique, when available, as cornerstone of current oncology guidelines.3,4 A drop in LVEF of >10% points to <50% during cancer regimens is defined as cardiotoxicity (overt cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction, CTRCD). Repeatedly, the day-to-day and loading condition induced variability of ejection fraction (EF) has been documented, as well as inherent limitations of the EF measurements (e.g. apical foreshortening, border delineation).5 Therefore, before interruption decisions or dosage limitation of chemotherapy EF should be reconfirmed after 2–3 weeks.3 In contrast, speckle tracking derived strain calculates the systolic deformation of the myocardium reflecting its contractile function.6 The prognostic usefulness especially of global longitudinal strain (GLS) in unveiling early subclinical impairment of left ventricular function, importantly preceding reduction in EF, has been corroborated in a variety of myocardial diseases and in cardio-oncology, if image quality is sufficient, despite vendor and software standard differences in acquired values.6,7 In cancer surveillance, strain has emerged as particularly rewarding, with a reduction from baseline GLS of >15% demonstrated to predict early and reliably the development of overt cardiotoxicity even in still preserved EF and is incorporated in the current position recommendations.3,8 Patients receiving potentially cardiotoxic oncology therapies are considered at high risk of heart failure [Stage A, American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) classification], shown to transition to heart failure Stage B in a significant percentage of about 20% of patients with different cancer entities in a recent report.9 In the present study of Santoro et al.10 in 116 women with HER2-positive breast cancer, serial echocardiography with 2D-GLS and LV EF was assessed every 3 months while undergoing a standard adjuvant chemotherapy protocol with the anthracycline epirubicin and cyclophosphamide, followed by paclitaxel and trastuzumab cycles. Patients without previous heart disease were included, and the mean age was 52.5 years. Overt CTRCD was defined as a decrease in EF >10% points to a value <50%, and subclinical CTRCD as a drop in GLS >15% independently of EF values, in accordance with the current European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging/American Society of Echocardiography consensus.8 In overt CTRCD, echocardiography was repeated after 2–3 weeks to confirm the ongoing EF reduction and patients were discussed together with the oncologists for decision whether discontinuation or adaptation of anti-cancer drugs was indicated, especially in the presence of cardiac symptoms.3 Importantly, it was implemented in the protocol design that all women showing either a subclinical CTRCD with GLS drop or overt cardiotoxicity with EF reduction promptly and immediately received cardiac heart failure therapy with the angiotensin converting enzyme-inhibitors ramipril and beta-blocker carvedilol. A relatively high average dose of ramipril could be achieved, titrated to 7.8 ± 2.5 mg, accompanied by carvedilol in a somewhat lower dose of 10.3 ± 3.1 mg, without any significant side effects despite the ongoing cancer treatments. The event of combined CTRCD occurred in almost every fourth woman (23%), in every fifth patient (20%) subclinical CTRCD was observed and appeared across the whole age range of 24–73 years. Due to subsequent overt CTRCD in only 3.4% of patients, chemotherapy needed to be interrupted based on EF reduction <50% and symptoms, e.g. dyspnoea only in few patients. Notably, GLS was reduced by <15% in all patients with CTRCD. Twice as many patients developed CTRCD during the trastuzumab protocol, after the anthracycline period was already absolved. Congruently, trastuzumab has been shown to potentiate cardiomyocyte damage after anthracyclines through a ‘dual-hit’ mechanism, including the inhibition of the neuregulin-1 survival signalling pathway for cardiac repair.11 Most importantly, in the current study, all patients with subclinical GLS reduction were able to complete their chemotherapy regimens with the pinpointed initiation of cardio-protective medication without further progression of cardiotoxicity, and three-fourth of patients with overt CTRCD could continue their oncology protocols due to recovery after start of concomitant cardiac therapy.10 Only one patient showed no recovery despite cardiac treatment. These prospective results enforce the concept that serial GLS measurements can (i) unmask early deterioration of the myocardium during cancer therapy, (ii) serve as easy guidance to start specific heart failure medication, and (iii) most importantly, avert interruption of the life-saving curative cancer treatment.10 Previous heart disease was excluded in the enrolment although more frequently encountered in elder women, as possible limitation of the applicability.10 However, it appears reasonable that an additional drop in strain in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease would be even more indicative of further cardiac damage induced through the oncologic therapy and should actuate intensified cardiac treatment. Hypertension when treated appropriately, did not appear to play a significant role in the development of cardiotoxicity in the present study. Remarkably, even in women not developing the cardiotoxicity cut-off definition of CTRCD, a statistically significant, albeit small reduction in systolic EF and/or GLS, as well as trend to diastolic impairment was observed at the end of the anthracycline/trastuzumab protocol treatments. These findings are in accordance with the observation that anthracyclines result in transcriptional activation of collagen synthesis leading to cardiac fibrosis confirmed in a translational animal model.12 An ongoing large multicentre international trial will randomize patients to EF- or strain imaging guidance strategies for the use of cardioprotective therapy during chemotherapy to determine cardiac outcome.13 In conclusion, strain monitoring with GLS guided initiation of targeted cardiac medication permits the continuation of chemotherapy without transition to overt heart failure and can avoid necessitating interruption of the crucial oncology treatments. The strain comparison should be performed with the same echocardiography vendor machines to avoid interaction of software differences, and GLS based on three apical views remains the preferred technique for cardiotoxicity detection.14 Cardio-oncology is a rapidly evolving field to further step up the ladder of survival strategies. Preventing later heart disease while curing the malignant disease is the aim and strain echocardiography is now bringing it closer to reality. Conflict of interest: none declared. title: Modeling of Heart Failure with Cyclophosphamide
abstract: The article presents the results of reproduction of the cyclophosphane model of heart failure. Outbred mice weighing 18–26 g at the onset of the experiment were used. All mice were divided into two groups with 10 animals in each. The first group was injected intraperitoneally with cyclophosphamide at a dose of 15 mg/kg, five times for 21 days (day 1, 5, 10, 15, and 21). The second group was intact animals. EchoCG was performed on the animals twice: baseline before the experiment (point 1) and one week after the last injection (point 2, day 28). The presented experimental model may be used for the study of drug toxicity prevention methods, as well as a model of heart failure with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction.

title: Senescence-based predicted potency of extracellular vesicles determines their rejuvenating cardiac effects in an ageing rodent model
abstract: Abstract Funding Acknowledgements Type of funding sources: Public grant(s) – National budget only. Main funding source(s): Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación CIBERCV Background Cardiac ageing is characterized by increased cell senescence, hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, which can frequently lead to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Still, this is an unmet medical need for treatment development. Cardiosphere-derived cells (CDCs) have demonstrated efficacy in old animals with cardiac dysfunction, however variability of effect among different CDC-donors is observed. Purpose To identify if the in vitro anti-senescent potential of CDC-secreted extracellular vesicles (CDC-EVs) predicts the in vivo anti-senescent effect in a model of cardiac ageing. Methods CDCs were derived from cardiac biopsies of 18 patients (age range 0 - 81 years old, both sexes included) who underwent cardiac surgery for other reasons. CDC-secreted extracellular vesicles (CDC-EVs) from the 18 donors were purified and used in vitro and in vivo experiments. Their in vitro anti-senescent potential (at genetic, secretory and cellular level) was evaluated over cardiac stromal cells from two human patients. CDC-EVs with the most anti-senescent potential and with the least anti-senescent potential were classified as potent (P-EVs) and non-potent (NP-EVs), respectively. Cardiac anti-senescent effect of P-EVs and NP-EVs were then tested in vivo in rats with induced cardiac aging. 3-months old SD-rats (30% female) received 3-months of daily intraperitoneal injections of saline (healthy control) or D-galactose. Animals in the D-Gal group were randomly allocated to receive intraperitoneal injection of saline (sham control, n=12), P-EVs (n=7) or NP-EVs (n=6) and followed-up for one month. Results Variations in the extent of the anti-senescent potential were observed in vitro among the CDC-EVs from the different donors. While most CDC-EVs significantly reduced cellular senescence and increased IL-6 secretion of human cardiac stromal cells, most CDC-EVs decreased the expression of senescence-related genes (p21, p16, p53, TGF-b). In vivo, D-gal induced cardiac hypertrophy (2.5 mg/g vs. 2.2 mg/g, p<0.01). P-EVs, but not NP-EVs, prevented this hypertrophy (2.4 vs. 2.9 mg/gr, p=0.05). This finding was in parallel to the levels of galactosidase-beta 1 expression in cardiac tissue, which were increased in sham vs healthy (1.22 vs. 0.78, p=0.04) and in sham vs. P-EVs (1.22 vs. 0.73, p=0.03) but levels in NP-EVs were not significantly different to the sham group (0.86, p=0.1). Conclusions The anti-senescent in vitro effect of CDC-EVs is correlated to their anti-senescent and anti-hypertrophic effect in an in vivo model of cardiac ageing. This study shows the relevance of exploring senescence-related markers as determinant of therapeutic potency of the tested product and confirms the potential utility of CDC-EVs as a therapy for cardiac ageing-related pathologies.
